tips.title: Ganache Components: Liquid, Butter, Sugar, and Additives
tips.docx:
TEXTURE
▪ thanks to the cocoa butter, ganache becomes fluid when heated and sets when cooled (due to the crystallization of cocoa butter molecules)
▪the lower the cocoa butter content and the higher the sugar content are, the softer the consistency of the ganache is

- for making ganache the chocolate should contain at least 18% cocoa butter and 40-70% cocoa products (these figures are usually indicated by manufacturers on the packaging)

- By cocoa products I mean the content of cocoa butter and cocoa mass (cocoa powder).

TASTE
▪ characteristic flavor of chocolate:

- white – sweet milky
- milk – vanilla-caramel
- dark – rich chocolate

▪ characteristic chocolate bitterness: it reinforces in ganache due to the increased content of cocoa products (70% or more) and is leveled when the content of cocoa products is around 50% (medium).
part 3

#marusya_about_ganache

Apart from chocolate, ganache must contain liquid. But here is where it gets fun: you can use different liquids, e.g:

- Fresh or pasteurized cream

The fat content of cream should be 35-40%. Thanks to minimal heat treatment, the finished ganache will have a rich creamy taste, but at the same time ‒ a reduced shelf life.

- Sterilized or UHT cream

The fat content is 35-37%. These types of cream are exposed to high temperatures for a short period of time. This process extends the product's shelf life making these creams chefs’ favorites when working with ganaches.

Milk
Is used to replace some or all of the cream in ganache. Unsweetened condensed milk (also called evaporated or concentrated milk) is often used to reduce the amount of water added, which negatively affects the shelf life of the ganache.

- Fruit or berry puree

Part of the cream can be replaced with puree. Most often, the ratio of puree and cream is 1:1. It is added to give ganache a fruity flavor and aroma, as well as interesting vivid colors.

DOSAGE
▫milk: maximum 40%
▫cream: 20-50%
▫puree: maximum 50%

How the liquid added affects the ganache?

TEXTURE
◽ gives the ganache a silky, melting texture during tasting (provided the fat content is at least 35%)
◽ in some cases, e.g. when preparing whipped ganache, cream is a necessary element for increasing the volume, as well as trapping and stabilizing air bubbles in the finished ganache

MOISTURE CONTENT
◽ liquid with a water content of about 60% dissolves sugar and makes the chocolate less dense

TASTE
▫ due to the fat molecules present in the composition, it has aroma-retaining properties and is a carrier of taste to our receptors
Part 4

So, did you miss this series of posts?

Today we continue talking about ganaches and as usual, I’m ready to share with you a concentrate of the best information from top pastry chefs and chocolatiers, seen through the prism of my experience and critical thinking.

Check out the beginning here #marusya_about_ganache

We’ve already analyzed the chocolate and liquid in the composition of ganache in detail, now let's move on to possible additives.

Butter
- fat content — 82% and more — the more fat contained in butter, the longer the shelf life of the finished ganache will be
- the butter is added when the ganache is at 32–34ºС

- dose — 5–15%

- recommended dose of fats (butter + cocoa butter) — 25–40% — too much fats will destabilize the ganache (the emulsion will break), while insufficient amount of fats will result in a ganache that’s too thick

When added to a ganache, the butter influences its:

TEXTURE
▪when the butter is heated, the consistency of the ganache becomes runnier, and when it cools, the ganache becomes thicker
▪makes the ganache smooth and creamy, adds it a glossy shine, as well as a delicate, melt-in-the mouth texture (provided the butter is added at the end of cooking, at 30-35ºС, without prior melting).

TASTE
▪ has aroma-retaining properties and is a carrier of taste to our receptors due to fat molecules in the composition
▪ reduces the bitterness of chocolate with a high content of cocoa products, e.g., >70%.

SHELF LIFE
▪ adding butter to cream before boiling it prolongs the shelf life of the ganache, and also contributes to the even distribution of fat molecules in the mixture.
Part 5

#marusya_about_ganache

In the previous part we discussed all the nuances of adding butter to a ganache. But apart from it, the following ingredients can be added to the ganache, namely:

Sugar
- sugar in ganaches can be represented by: sucrose (=sugar), invert sugar or glucose syrup (high in dextrose)
- dose — at least 25% of the total weight

When added to a ganache, sugar influences its:

TASTE
▪makes the ganache sweeter

TEXTURE
▪makes it softer and more elastic
▪increases the viscosity of the ganache, making it more stable due to its hygroscopic properties

SHELF LIFE
▪ prolongs shelf life — sugar helps to “bind” water present in cream, making it unavailable for the microorganisms (molds) to multiply.

- Sorbitol or food supplement E420
It is an odorless white crystalline powder with a pleasant taste. It is two times less sweet than regular sugar and is very hygroscopic (absorbs and retains moisture).
- dose — 1.5–2.5% of the total weight

The way sorbitol affects the ganache is similar to sugar, however, E420 is used primarily as a stabilizer, and not as a sweetener.

Aromatic additives
- can be represented by various extracts, essential oils, alcohol, as well as flavored cream or milk
- all additives that are sensitive to microflora (cocoa powder, spices, etc.) should be boiled for several minutes along with the cream
Part 6 and last

Guys, have you missed us?

‘cause we missed you immensely!

Inspired after a short vacation, we are preparing new wow-materials for you!

Today I’d like to share with you the last piece of information about ganaches in order you could round up all the information you already learnt and arrange it into a coherent picture.

We have already discussed with you what ganache is, what it can consist of and what are the possible additives, and we also examined in detail each basic component separately: the recommended dosage of the ingredient and its influence on the texture, taste and shelf life of the ganache.

Check out the beginning here #marusya_about_ganache

Today I will share with you a couple more useful tips and tricks.

- Why has your ganache split?

1. It doesn't contain enough liquid
2. Poor dispersion of fats in water
3. Indoor temperature is too high

🆘 How to fix split ganache?

1. Add heavy cream/milk/puree
2. Process the mixture with a hand blender
3. Process the mixture with a hand blender and allow it to cool

And here comes another interesting nuance:

- Ganache should be processed with a hand blender while it is hot to avoid air bubbles getting into the mixture! This is due to the fact that:

- air is a favorable environment for microorganisms
- fats that are in contact with air eventually turn rancid

- How and how long can ganache be stored?

- Before storing and cooling the ganache, it should be covered with cling film that comes in contact with the surface of the ganache. This way, you will protect your ganache from air, microorganisms and evaporation of aromatic substances.

- Ganaches can be stored in the fridge at 4ºС for no more than 2 days. You can freeze them only in finished products.

tips.title: WHY DO YOU NEED TO SIFT THE FLOUR?
tips.docx:
Almost every pastry recipe calls for sifted flour. Have you ever thought about why you should sift it?

Let's start with what we have actually moved away from for a long time, thanks to modern production technologies.

In the past, it was always necessary to sift the flour in order to:

▪ get rid of weevils and other bugs
- Nowadays contaminated foods should be disposed immediately.
▪ get rid of the smallest pieces of stone for grinding grain — quern. The saddle quern consisted of a flat stone bed and a rounded stone to be operated manually against it; later, millstones developed from those hand-operated querns
▪ get rid of debris — threads from packing bags, cereals from a neighboring box, pieces of paper or plastic bags, etc.

Nowadays, here are a few times you should sift your flour for baking:

▪ to eliminate and prevent lumps — when your flour has been sitting around for a while, seems to be tightly packed, or has been stored at high humidity, lumps form even in high-quality flour.
▪ to get a homogeneous, uniform base for the dough — sifted flour mixes better with other ingredients, and the dough behaves more predictably
▪ to get much lighter and airier flour — it’s especially important when baking sponges
▪ to guarantee you get the right amount when the recipe uses cups instead of grams as a unit of measure (American recipes) — sifted flour will have a larger volume than not sifted

### Lifehack from Marusya

If the flour you are using is fairly fresh and does not contain any lumps, in most cases you can skip sifting, and make your flour airier simply by mixing it with a whisk.

tips.title: Honey Cake Layers: Factors That Affect the Intensity of Honey Taste and Aroma
tips.docx:
HONEY CAKE LAYERS: FACTORS THAT AFFECT THE INTENSITY OF HONEY TASTE AND AROMA

Honey cake layers can have a different intensity of honey taste and aroma: from delicate, subtle honey notes to strong, pronounced ones. What does it depend on?

The very first and seemingly obvious answer that comes to mind is the amount of honey added. But in fact, this is far from the primary factor.

1. The intensity of the honey taste and aroma in the cake layers depends primarily on the heat treatment the batter undergoes before baking — the more you heat the honey mixture, the more pronounced taste will have the cake layers:

- subtle honey taste and aroma can be obtained by bringing the mixture for the honey dough to 60–70 °C over a water bath or in a saucepan
- moderately pronounced taste is obtained by bringing the honey or the honey mixture to a boil (100–116 °C)
- rich, pronounced honey taste and aroma of the cake layers is achieved by boiling the honey mixture or by using the dough made with burnt honey (> 116 °C)

2. Secondly, the intensity of the honey taste and aroma of the cake layers depends on the type of honey. If you want to get cakes with a light, delicate honey taste, opt for light types of honey, for example, acacia or linden. Buckwheat honey and other dark types should be preferred if you like cakes with a rich, pronounced honey taste.

3. The amount of honey added to the dough makes less difference to the intensity of honey taste and aroma of cake layers compared to the type of honey and its heat treatment. Therefore, do not be surprised that the amount of honey in honey recipes can vary from 60 to 450 g, depending on the recipe.

P.S. The photos show the Pear–Gorgonzola–Pine Nut honey cake, which drives fans of the sweet fragrant pear and noble blue cheese crazy.

Do you think the dough for this honey cake is cooked over a water bath or is brought to a boil? Those who vote for the water bath, type "1" in the comments, for boiling — type "2".

tips.title: BROWN VS. WHITE EGGS — IS THERE A DIFFERENCE?
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

Guys, you probably noticed that in some countries in supermarkets the prices for brown and white eggs differ? Is there any reason for that? Or is it just a marketing ploy?

Let's figure it out. But first things first.

Is there really a difference between brown and white eggs?

- Yes — in color

Eggs come in many colors, depending on the breed of the hen. Chickens have different pigment genes that determine the color of the egg shell. Generally speaking, white shell eggs come from hens with white feathers and white earlobes, while brown shell eggs are produced by hens with brown feathers and red earlobes.
- some chickens have a unique pigment gene and lay multi-colored eggs — light blue, green and even pink

- No — in terms of nutritional value and taste

The color of the eggshell is not indicative of the best quality of the egg. In fact, there is no distinguishable difference between brown and white eggs when it comes to taste and nutritional value.
- The nutritional value and palatability of an egg depend solely on the diet and environment of the chicken. The food eaten by the hen can directly affect how an egg tastes, which means that pasture-raised hens usually lay eggs that have a richer taste and higher concentration of useful macro- and microelements

- Is the higher price for brown eggs a marketing ploy?

- No — hens with brown feathers tend to be larger than hens with white feathers, meaning they consume more feed. Therefore, brown eggs need to be sold at a higher price to make up for the extra costs

- Yes — if you have faced an unscrupulous dealer speculating on their more "natural" appearance

tips.title: FLAVOR PAIRING. PASSION FRUIT
tips.docx:
#marusya_flavor_pairing

In winter, more than ever, we crave sunny desserts and bright summer flavors, although passion fruit is popular all year round. It is valued for its rich taste and aroma, which gives desserts a special charm. Let's figure out what to combine this exotic fruit with.

- tart and sweet
- refreshing
- a hint of herbaceousness in seeds
- has juicy pulp
- top fruity notes
- slightly tart aftertaste

It is impossible to describe the flavor of passion fruit in one word. It combines the freshness of kiwi, the tartness of sea buckthorn, the airy sweetness of peach and apricot, the juiciness of gooseberries, the tartness of plums and the tenderness of strawberries — a nice cocktail of rich sweet and tart taste.

- fragrant fruity aroma
- peach notes
- light tropical sweetness
- unique floral notes
- balsamic undertones
- a hint of woody notes

Pairs well with:

- nuts — macadamia, almonds, cashews

- alcoholic drinks — rum, tequila, wine and all kinds of citrus liqueurs, for example, Cointreau — a French liqueur with the sweet orange peel and bitter orange aroma

- dairy products — heavy cream, mascarpone, cream cheese

tips.docx:
start by tag #marusya_about_butter

Well, the start of a new week! Wish you all the best and a productive Monday!

Today I’ve prepared a continuation about the types of butter. Learn, save it to your bookmarks and don’t forget to leave your and any comment under the post — I will be very pleased!

So, we have already talked about sweet cream, salted, compound and ghee butter. There are 4 more types left.

### Cultured butter

This is the secret ingredient in the best bakery products! This type of butter is obtained by adding pure cultures of lactic acid bacteria to cream (hence the European name cultured butter) and fermentation of the mixture for at least 24 hours. In the process of the fermentation we obtain a thick product with a pronounced cultured milk aroma that enhances the flavor of dishes with the addition of butter, such as pancakes, pies or mashed potatoes.

### European-style butter

European butter can boast about its high fat content of 82% to 90%. The high fat content with longer-lasting whipping and live cultures gives European butter a bright yellow color and rich flavor that is instantly transferred to bakery products.

### Whipped butter

This fresh look at a traditional butter involves adding air to it to create an easy-to-butter ingredient. Using a hand or planetary mixer make creamy whipped butter that keeps its smooth texture even after cooling. You can also add milk for a softer consistency. Put whipped butter on a crispy piece of baguette and enjoy a restaurant-worthy snack!

### Brown butter (beurre noisette)

Brown butter is an ultra-luxury ingredient that adds a nice nutty flavor to everything from bread and cake to Brussels sprouts. Heating of diced sweet cream butter until the milk solids begin to turn brown gives a toasted and delicious butter that is incredibly fragrant in both liquid and solid form.

tips.docx:
#marusya_flavor_pairing

Today I reveal the food pairing secrets of coffee

▪ complex
▪ rich
▪ earthy
▪ has a characteristic bitterness
▪ floral notes
▪ nutty flavor
▪ specific astringent aftertaste

The flavor of coffee can vary greatly depending on its place of origin, processing method, degree of roasting and brewing.

▪ refreshing exquisite fragrance
▪ has a characteristic smell of freshly dug earth/soil after downpour
▪ woody notes
▪ hints of fruity aroma
▪ sweet spicy notes
▪ inherent slight oiliness

Over 800 aromatic components have been identified in roasted coffee beans!

Pairs well with:

- nuts — pecans, almonds, pistachios and walnuts

But it forms the most spectacular pair with hazelnuts — it contains butanedione (diacetyl), which gives a characteristic oily flavor — the same molecule is found in coffee. Therefore, there is nothing surprising in the fact that Nutty Latte Cheesecake (photo 3-4) has become one of the top flavors!

- other fruits and berries such as blackcurrant, cherry, orange, pomegranate and blackberry

Coffee contains volatile aldehydes and esters, giving it a floral notes and hints of sweet spices like cloves. The banana flavor also contains floral and clove components, so that the two flavors merge into a unity that is pleasant for everyone.

- spices and herbs — cloves, coriander, vanilla, cinnamon, ginger, lavender.

- chocolate is always a winning combination! Coffee goes well with both milk and dark chocolate. But white chocolate will give it special elegance and nobility — the bitterness of coffee gives a pronounced contrast with white chocolate.

- alcoholic drinks — cognac, brandy, spiced rum, as well as all kinds of liqueurs: almond "Amaretto", berry "Creme de Cassis" based on blackcurrant and, of course, Irish cream liqueur "Baileys" — Coffee-Baileys Cheesecake beat all sales records (photo 5-6)

tips.title: HOW TO RECALCULATE THE CHOCOLATE PERCENTAGE
tips.docx:
#marusya_about_chocolate

More than enough times, I've been faced with complaints about broken ganache and tearful pleas for help.

I will help.

In 99% of cases, beginners simply replace the amount of chocolate specified in the recipe with exactly the same amount of chocolate with a different percentage of cocoa products.

json.title: HOW TO RECALCULATE THE CHOCOLATE PERCENTAGE
json.text:
#marusya_about_chocolate

More than enough times, I've been faced with complaints about broken ganache and tearful pleas for help.

I will help.

In 99% of cases, beginners simply replace the amount of chocolate specified in the recipe with exactly the same amount of chocolate with a different percentage of cocoa products.

tips.title: DON’T DO THIS
tips.docx:
Is it possible basically to replace one chocolate with another?

- Yes, if you correctly calculate the required amount of chocolate with a cocoa butter content that is different from that specified in the recipe

Let's say the recipe says 400 g of dark chocolate 54% (chocolate A). You only have 64% chocolate (Chocolate B) available.

How to recalculate?

The 54% marking reflects the total content of cocoa products (cocoa butter and cocoa liquor). For instance, 100 g of 54% chocolate may contain 45 g of sugar (45%), 19 g of cocoa liquor (19%) and 36 g of cocoa butter (36%).
- see the cocoa butter content on the package or clarify with the manufacturer

Enter the factor value

factor = cocoa butter content/100

The recipe uses 400 g of 54% chocolate (which is 19% cocoa liquor and 36% cocoa butter), and you want to replace it with 64% chocolate, which contains 41% cocoa butter

factor A (chocolate 54%) = 36% (cocoa butter)/100 = 0.36
factor B (chocolate 64%) = 41% (cocoa butter)/100 = 0.41

We have calculated the factor value for both types of chocolate, now we need to calculate how much of the available chocolate 64% we will need, according to the formula:

x = (weight of chocolate A * factor A) / factor B

Substitute the values:

x = (400 g * 0.36) / 0.41 = 351 g

That is, you can replace 400 g of 54% chocolate with 351 g of 64% chocolate that you have available.

tips.title: 8 TYPES OF BUTTER AND HOW TO USE THEM
tips.docx:
#marusya_about_butter

Any butter is made from cream. But depending on the origin of the cream, the composition of the butter and ways of preparation, there are several varieties that ensure different tastes of meals and serve for different purposes:

### Sweet Cream Butter (Unsalted Butter)

It is the most popular variety due to its versatility: it can be used both for frying vegetables, meat, and for making desserts and pastries. It is made only from cream of animal origin.

### Salted Butter

Unsalted butter is all cream, while the salted variety has some salt added. Salt acts as a preservative, so this variety of butter lasts longer than the unsalted one. Most often, it is used for spreading on bread, topping veggies and pasta.

### Ghee butter

Gee is nothing more than the pure butterfat! It is cooked over low heat to remove the water molecules until the milk solids brown lightly, creating a slightly nutty, caramelized aroma. Ghee butter is shelf-stable and has a high smoke point. It is most commonly used for sautéing vegetables, meat, but it’s also used in baked goods thanks to its rich flavor.

### Compound butter

This is a special variety of butter that has been softened to a pliable state, and then has herbs, spices, and/or sweeteners (fruit or berry purees) added to it. Usually chilled and then sliced, compound butter can add herby richness to a steak, enhance the flavor of a baked good, or add creaminess to a pasta sauce.

There are 4 types of food salt:

▫table salt

They differ from each other in the methods of harvesting, chemical composition — and, accordingly, taste, as well as varying degrees of salinity, depending on the content of sodium chloride in the composition.

rock salt

They differ from each other in the methods of harvesting, chemical composition — and, accordingly, taste, as well as varying degrees of salinity, depending on the content of sodium chloride in the composition.

tips.title: TABLE SALT
tips.docx:
The most commonly used variety of salt. Most table salt is mined, then put into water, purified of other trace minerals and re-dehydrated (evaporated). The content of NaCl is no less than 97% on a dry matter basis.

There are different grades of table salt:

- second
- first
- top
- "Extra"

The main feature of "Extra" grade is that it is fine-grained (almost like a powder) and often comes in "iodized" form which means it includes a small amount of potassium iodide or sodium iodide. The addition of iodine does not change the taste of the salt itself, but when heated above 100 °C, iodized salt decomposes and gives a dish a metallic aftertaste.

"Extra" grade salt has a distinctive taste. Such salt is convenient to use in food production: its high degree of salinity and low cost reduce the cost of purchasing and storing the product.

tips.title: SEA SALT
tips.docx:
A type of salt of natural (marine) origin, extracted from seawater through the use of a vacuum evaporation process after which it is sun and wind dried and then distilled into an edible, solid form. The purity of sea salt depends on the composition and purity of the sea water from which it is harvested.

Sea salt not only enhances the taste of foods, but can also add different flavors depending on the additives in its composition. It is much less salty than table or rock salt, so when cooking, you need much more of it to make the dish salty.

▫Fleur de Sel ("flower of salt" in French)
The most expensive among sea salts. It has an exceptional taste and is able to give dishes a special delicacy and sophistication. This salt has snowflake-like crystals which add a crunchy texture to dishes.

tips.title: LAKE SALT
tips.docx:
It is extracted from the bottom of salt lakes, where it settles naturally. Then it undergoes purification processes, after which the salt crystals are converted into food salt. Lake salt has a low sodium chloride content, so it is considered less salty.

Classification of salt on the basis of salinity levels from higher to lower:

1. Table salt "Extra" grade
2. Table salt of the first, second and top grades
3. Rock salt
4. Sea salt
5. Lake salt

In all my recipes I use rock salt. Therefore, if you use any other type of salt, make sure to reduce / increase its amount based on the degree of salinity.
part 3 and last

Today we will figure out how much salt should be added to desserts and pastries, and we will also talk about what kind of salt is used in confectionery.

How much salt to add? This usually depends on:

◾ variety of salt
We have already figured out that, first and foremost, the amount of salt added to dessert depends on the type of salt you use, since each of them has a different degree of salinity. You can read about it in detail by following the hashtag #marusya_about_salt

◾ goal you want to achieve
If you want just to enhance the taste of the dessert, then you will need less salt than to eliminate excessive sweetness, for example.

◾ your taste preferences
Depending on taste buds, a dessert with the same amount of salt will be moderately salty for some, and slightly over-salted for others.

- Basic ratios of salt to flour and sugar:
1/4 tsp. salt per cup (130 g) flour
1/4 tsp. salt per cup (180 g) sugar

If the dessert you are making contains both flour and sugar, then first use salt in ratio only to the ingredient that weighs more, check the result, and then add more salt if necessary.

- Which variety of salt to use in pastry?
When choosing the type of salt to add, think of the goal you want to achieve:

◾ if you need salt to decorate your dessert, then opt for Fleur de Sel — it has snowflake-like crystals and ennobles the dessert with its crispy texture. Other varieties of sea salt that have a crystalline structure are also suitable for decoration.

◾ to enhance the taste of the dessert, I advise you to use rock or sea salt. They dissolve well in the dough and don’t add bitterness, which is typical of iodized and table salt.

◾ if you use salt as a bitterness neutralizer, why add an extra bitter taste along with table salt?

tips.title: WHY ADD SALT TO DESSERTS?
tips.docx:
part 1

When I began to study this question, it immediately became clear that for this topic I’ll need more than one post. You may wonder what salt has to do with dessert. Let’s have a look.

Firstly, in some cases it’s really impossible to make a dessert without salt. Secondly, without it, most of sweet pastries become insipid.

Let's figure it out.

json.title: WHY ADD SALT TO DESSERTS?
json.text:
part 1

When I began to study this question, it immediately became clear that for this topic I’ll need more than one post. You may wonder what salt has to do with dessert. Let’s have a look.

Firstly, in some cases it’s really impossible to make a dessert without salt. Secondly, without it, most of sweet pastries become insipid.

Let's figure it out.

tips.title: FUNCTIONS OF SALT IN BAKING AND MAKING DESSERTS
tips.docx:
1. Tightens the gluten structure

Salt has a binding or strengthening effect on gluten — this allows the dough to rise and expand during baking. It’s indispensable, for example, when baking bread, pastries, croissants or sponges.

- It’s impossible to get a tall sponge without adding salt to the batter. Salted batter will turn out more voluminous and stronger than unsalted.

2. Enhances the taste

Salt brings out the characteristic taste of pastry it is used in. When used in moderate amounts, it does not make the product taste salty, but simply enhances its best qualities. It turns insipid two-dimensional tastes into rich, three-dimensional ones.

Such an effect is achieved thanks to the right combination of different tastes. For example, when salt is added, sweet flavors become less sweet and more complex, while sour flavors become less prominent.

3. Neutralize bitterness

Salt neutralizes bitterness, so any bitter foods (e.g. coffee, dark chocolate, grapefruit) become more appetizing and tasty if you add a little salt.

- Grapefruit remains slightly bitter both fresh and baked even after removing the albedo (the whitish, spongy inner part of the rind of a citrus fruit). But salting the pulp helps to get rid of this specific aftertaste.

4. Stabilizes the egg white foam

It’s thanks to the addition of that tiny pinch of salt that the egg whites, when whipped, start to increase in volume and become lush. Adding salt to your meringue will ensure that all of the protein chains have safely bonded together.

A similar effect can be obtained by adding acid (e.g. lemon juice).

json.text:
1. Tightens the gluten structure

Salt has a binding or strengthening effect on gluten — this allows the dough to rise and expand during baking. It’s indispensable, for example, when baking bread, pastries, croissants or sponges.

Salt brings out the characteristic taste of pastry it is used in. When used in moderate amounts, it does not make the product taste salty, but simply enhances its best qualities. It turns insipid two-dimensional tastes into rich, three-dimensional ones.

tips.title: HOT METHOD
tips.docx:
Many of you, probably, have guessed that the hot method involves heat treatment. You’re on the right track. Hot infusion consists in bringing the liquid together with spices, herbs or other flavorings to a boil, followed by infusion for 30-60 minutes.

The infused liquid can be cream, milk or berry puree. For example, you can infuse the cream with dry lavender, as I did in Blueberry-Lavender Cheesecake (photo 3-6), or you can give a mouthwatering coffee aroma by hot infusion the cream with ground coffee (Coffee-Baileys Cheesecake, photo 7-8).

Everything is very simple, but there are secrets that I will gladly share with you.

json.title: HOT METHOD
json.text:
Many of you, probably, have guessed that the hot method involves heat treatment. You’re on the right track. Hot infusion consists in bringing the liquid together with spices, herbs or other flavorings to a boil, followed by infusion for 30-60 minutes.

The infused liquid can be cream, milk or berry puree. For example, you can infuse the cream with dry lavender, as I did in Blueberry-Lavender Cheesecake (photo 3-6), or you can give a mouthwatering coffee aroma by hot infusion the cream with ground coffee (Coffee-Baileys Cheesecake, photo 7-8).

Everything is very simple, but there are secrets that I will gladly share with you.

tips.title: HOT METHOD SECRETS
tips.docx:
- The infused liquid must be heated over medium or low heat so that the heating occurs gradually.
- In the infusion process, I advise you to use as few dishes as possible to prepare ingredients. For example, it is better to remove the zest immediately into cream. Don’t remove the zest on the board, and then transfer it to cream from the board, as all spices, herbs and citrus fruits contain a large amount of essential oils which evaporate easily.
- After boiling, you must immediately remove the saucepan from the heat - at too high temperatures, flavors can release substances that will negatively affect the flavor and aroma.
- After heating, it is better to cover the liquid with a cling film in contact. If you cover it with a lid, excess moisture from evaporation will form on it, which will get into the liquid. Furthermore, skin which you will need to remove will be formed.
- After infusion, don’t forget to strain it through a sieve or cheesecloth.
- The infused liquid can be stored in the refrigerator after complete cooling during the shelf life of the main product. Keep in mind that the resulting flavor will evaporate with each day of storage!

Did you learn something new for yourself today? If yes, let me know in the comments
5. Balances sweetness

Salt helps to balance the taste of products with a pronounced sweetness, such as caramel, chocolate or meringue. Such products are usually treacly, and it’s almost impossible to add other flavor accents to them, even if you think they will work well in your pastry. Salt added in low concentrations balances the sweetness and adds depth to other flavors, so that our taste buds perceive them as moderately sweet, although the amount of sugar remains unchanged.

6. Helps to release juices

Salt changes the balance of liquid in foods. It makes juicy berries and fruits release juices, leaving the fibrous material behind. If you are making a fruit dessert and you need to get the maximum juice, just add a pinch of salt to your fruits.

7. Increases the shelf life

Salt is a natural preservative. It dehydrates harmful microorganisms. Due to dehydration, bacteria become inactive, their growth stops, the metabolism of their cells becomes impossible, which is why they die. Different types of microorganisms become harmless at different salt concentrations. But even in a small amount, salt increases the shelf life of pastry.

8. Helps to maintain the recommended daily sodium intake

Our body needs a certain amount of salt (NaCl) to function properly, so it's natural that we tend to like the taste of salt. This does not mean that we should eat tons of salt a day, but using it in reasonable amounts in cooking and making desserts will help us stay healthy and enjoy food.

part 4 (the last one)

We have already talked with you about the cold and hot method of infusion. Today I will tell you about decoction and vacuuming.

tips.title: DECOCTION
tips.docx:
This method, of course, is very similar to hot method — the liquid is also subjected to heat treatment. However, there is one significant difference — with hot method, we only heat the liquid or bring it to a boil, but as for decoction, we boil for several minutes or even cook for up to 60 minutes to get dense aromatic decoctions.
Infusions are steeped and decoctions are simmered.

If we talk about confectionery, this method is often used in the preparation of flavored sugar syrups for coating muffins or, for example, soaking sponge cake.

For the preparation of fillings for honey cakes "Fig-Parmesan-Gorgonzola-Red Wine" and "Quince-Goat Cheese-Medium Sweet White Wine" we also use this method — juicy fleshy figs and fragrant quince are stewed in wine from 25 to 60 minutes until the liquid has almost completely evaporated. Due to the prolonged exposure to high temperature, we get incredibly tasty, rich and fragrant fillings!

tips.title: VACUUMING
tips.docx:
This is a method for infusion of solid ingredients (bananas, mangoes, coconut, pineapple, apples, etc.), which are subsequently used as whole or cut.

Thanks to vacuuming, we can give the main product a lot of flavors!

There are several ways:

1. Take a dense main ingredient and pour it with juice of the infusing one, then leave to infuse in the refrigerator.
2. Mix the main and infusing ingredients — you can even wrap apple pieces with lemon slices or thin mango strips, sprinkled with cinnamon or other spices. After that, it is necessary to place them in a bag for vacuuming and pump out the air with a vacuum cleaner.

As a result, you can get an orange-flavored apple, for example, or a lemon-flavored banana.

tips.title: EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT AGAR
tips.docx:
part 1

In previous posts, we have already talked with you about gelatin - #marusya_about_gelatin and pectin - #marusya_about_pectin. Today I suggest analyzing the next, no less interesting thickener - agar, aka agar-agar, aka seaweed food thickener.

Agar means "seaweed" in Malaysian. Its gelling properties are said to be accidentally discovered in Japan in the 17th century by Mino Tarōzaemon. He found out that the chilled seaweed soup had a jelly-like consistency the next day.

Agar is extracted from red and brown algae, which undergo several stages of rinsing, drying and grinding.

Nowadays, this natural thickener is widely used in confectionery art. It’s used to make zephyr, marmalade, fruit pastes (pastila), sweets, jelly and mousse desserts.

Agar can be classified by its quality and gel strength.

### Quality

- High grade agar - has a white or light yellow color, although it can have a slightly grayish tint
- First grade agar - varies from yellow to dark yellow color

### Gel strength

- 600-1200 g/cm2

The higher the number it has, the thicker gel can be obtained. The greater the strength of agar is, the less amount of it is needed to gel the mixture.

- You can check out the table that shows how to convert between different amounts of agar-agar depending on the gel strength in the carousel.

Agar is often referred to as a natural substitute for gelatin. However, these two thickeners have a number of differences.

json.title: EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT AGAR
json.text:
part 1

In previous posts, we have already talked with you about gelatin - #marusya_about_gelatin and pectin - #marusya_about_pectin. Today I suggest analyzing the next, no less interesting thickener - agar, aka agar-agar, aka seaweed food thickener.

tips.title: AGAR VS GELATIN
tips.docx:
1. Unlike gelatin, agar does not impart any taste, smell, or color to desserts.
2. In terms of gelling properties, agar is 10 times superior to gelatin
3. Unlike gelatin, agar activates in an acidic environment. Gelatin is not a good choice when it comes to preparing, for example, desserts with pineapple or kiwi - they contain enzymes that destroy proteins (87-92% of the composition of gelatin). But agar-agar perfectly gels such mixtures.
4. Unlike gelatin, agar is thermoreversible - it can be heated and frozen as many times as you like.
part 2

Please support this useful post with your like ー this is extremely important for us now!

For those interested in the answer to the question from the previous post about using agar to make the orange confit for the “Orange-Dark Chocolate" honey cake: I chose it because the filling made with gelatin began to leak out after defrosting.

This is due to the fact that ice crystals formed in the orange confit during freezing, which broke the texture of the jelly. As a result, the filling lost its original properties and began to leak out after defrosting.

Will gelatin-based filling always leak out after defrosting? No, it won’t. Moreover, sometimes after defrosting, a filling made with agar or pectin may also leak out. What does it depend on? First of all, it depends on the amount of unbound water in the composition, but this should be discussed in another post.

Today we’ll continue examining the agar. So, here are the RULES OF WORKING WITH AGAR:

1. Agar does not dissolve in cold water ー it should be brought to 95-100 °C to completely dissolve, at this temperature it forms a viscous and transparent solution, which when cooled to 35-40 °C, turns into a thick and pure gel.

2. Agar does not require pre-soaking in water or mixing with sugar. In order to introduce agar into the mixture, it is enough just to add it in there! The mixture can be hot, warm or cold ー it does not matter.

3. Agar is a thermoreversible thickener. You can heat and freeze fillings made with it as many times as you like ー it won't lose its gelling properties.

4. One of the main advantages of agar over gelatin is the ability to activate in an acidic environment. The advantage over pectin is that agar gels well even in the absence of sugar in the mixture.

5. The thicker the desired consistency of the gel you want to obtain is, the stronger agar should be used and / or the more agar you need.
part 3

Today we’ll talk about how to correctly calculate the required amount of agar and what it depends on.

If you are making a dessert with agar using a recipe from an eminent chef, in order to get a stable result, be sure to pay attention to:

- amount of agar — agar is a very strong thickener (10 times stronger than gelatin), so even a slight deviation of 0.1-0.2 g can change the texture of the gel
- strength of agar — if the recipe says "5 g of agar 1200", to get a dessert "like from a chef" you need to either use agar of the same strength or use the one that is available and convert between its strength.

- you can find the table that shows how to convert between different amounts of agar-agar depending on the gel strength in the 1st post from the series #marusya_about_agar.

- agar brand (if specified) — as a rule, despite the same strength, agar of different brands can slightly differ in the opacity / transparency of the gel obtained and gelling properties, so it is best to stick to a brand recommended by chef.

If you use a recipe from the Internet, where there’s no information about the strength of the agar used, or you want to create a dessert yourself, take into account the following tips:

### Recommended dosage

2-4 g of agar per 150-180 ml of liquid

The exact amount depends on:

- liquid being gelled and its acidity

The higher the acidity of the liquid is, the more agar must be added. This is due to the fact that acid lowers the gelling properties of thickeners, including agar. For example, to gel 100 ml of a neutral liquid (e.g. water, milk) you’ll need 0.9-1 g of agar, while for 100 ml of an acidic liquid (e.g. juice) — 1.3-1.5 g of agar.

- desired texture

runny texture — 0.8 g / 500 ml
soft texture — 1.5 g / 500 ml
thick texture — 5 g / 500 ml
very thick texture — 7 g / 500 ml

If this post was useful for you, leave any comment or emoticon under it — I’ll be very pleased
#marusya_about_agar

part 4

Today will be the final part of a series of articles about agar. I’ll tell you about the terms and conditions of storage, as well as possible agar substitutes.

tips.title: TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF STORAGE
tips.docx:
### Agar

The shelf life of agar varies from 2 to 3 years since the date of packaging. It is indicated on the packaging and may change depending on the formula and production technology of agar by a specific manufacturer.

Agar should be stored in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight, in airtight packaging.

- Products with agar

1. Agar-based confectionery products are stored about 24 to 36 hours at a temperature between +4 to -8°C
2. Fruit mixtures — up to 7 days in the refrigerator
3. Jam and other preservation — up to 1 month in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight

tips.title: AGAR SUBSTITUTES
tips.docx:
### Gelatin

Gelatin has a lower density after cooling than agar, so it is suitable for making more delicate desserts. If you want to get a dense and smooth texture, it is better to use agar.

In general, these thickeners can be considered interchangeable, but it should be kept in mind that the gelling ability of agar is much higher than that of gelatin.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. gelatin

ℹ It’s not suitable for vegetarians, as gelatin is made from the bones and tendons of animals

### Pectin

Pectin is the most beneficial and equivalent substitute for agar, but there are exceptions. Both products have the vegetal nature and the only difference is that pectin contains carbohydrates, and its calorie content is higher than that of agar.

A prerequisite for the "activation" of pectin is the presence of sugar. Accordingly, substitute agar for pectin in the making of sugar-free desserts is impossible.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. pectin

### Corn Starch

Agar-agar can be substituted for starch. However, starch makes the filling opaque, when dissolved, that significantly narrows the range of its possibilities.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2 tsp. starch

tips.title: FLAVOR PAIRING. LEMON
tips.docx:
In the pastry art, lemon can be considered a versatile citrus fruit that not only serves as the basis for creating desserts with a characteristic lemon sourness, but also for balancing sweet and savory tastes.

Let's have a look at the flavor profile of LEMON

- sour
- pure, refreshing flavor dominated by citric acid

We feel the pronounced sourness of lemon precisely thanks to the lemon juice. But the rich bouquet of aromas that a lemon possesses is revealed when the zest is peeled.

- dominant citrus notes
- waxy and oily accents in essential oils and volatile compounds contained in the peel
- notes of rose, lavender and pine
- light grass, camphor, woody, pine tree aroma

Lemon is a natural flavor enhancer. For example, thanks to it, the taste of an orange becomes more expressive. It matches perfectly with:

- other fruits and berries such as orange, grapefruit, raspberry, blackberry, blueberry, mango, peach.

Lemon-blueberry is one of the most interesting combinations: the floral notes of blueberries are masked by its sour juice, and the acidity of the lemon doesn’t add to its floral aroma. But! When enough sugar or honey is added, both flavors reveal and create an incredible, aromatic combination in desserts.

- alcoholic drinks - red wine, gin, rum and orange liqueur. It stands out the most when paired with the Italian Limoncello liqueur.

- nuts - pecans, cashews, almonds, pistachios and walnuts

- herbs and spices - basil, cayenne pepper, poppy seeds, mint, thyme, rosemary

Lemon-ginger is one of the most successful and harmonious flavor combinations. This pair has very similar flavor profiles. And only your sense of smell will help you find the subtle differences between lemon flavor of ginger and ginger flavor of lemon.

That is why the Lemon-Ginger honey cake recipe gained such popularity. You can find this free recipe by following the hashtag #marusya_recipe

- Check out the carousel to see an aide-memoire on lemon flavor combinations

tips.docx:
#marusya_flavor_pairing

As you remember, we’ve started diving into the world of food pairing with apricot, and today I suggest having a closer look at MANGO.

- sweet-tart
- reminiscent of a pineapple and peach combination
- has citrus and floral notes

- creamy notes
- apricot and pineapple notes, melon flavor
- has a slightly pine/evergreen aroma with notes of dried fruits

Mango matches well the fruity, spiced and creamy flavors of other ingredients, but you should always make sure that this flavor does not dominate over the others. Perfectly pairs with:

- nuts - cashews, macadamia, almonds, hazelnuts

- herbs and spices - ginger, cardamom, coriander, jasmine, mint, basil and cilantro. Chef Richard Corrigan uses the mango-rhubarb combination in his dishes.

- dairy products - Emmental and brie cheese
- alcoholic drinks - Cointreau liqueur, Amaretto, cider and Kirsch

- other fruits and berries such as apricot, pineapple, cranberry, passion fruit, lemon.

The following flavor combinations deserve special attention:

- mango-coconut
An important role in ripe mango taste play lactone compounds that lend a coconut-like note perceived by the taste buds at the back of the tongue.

- mango-orange
Both mango and orange have a citrus-floral flavor, but when paired, orange is dominated by the complex flavor of mango, which has a slightly pine/evergreen aroma with notes of dried fruits, so after a while, the orange flavor becomes subtle.

- mango-lime
Fresh lime juice squeezed over a ripe mango is one of the world's greatest flavor combinations. The distinct zesty sour flavor of lime submits to the taste of mango with its floral notes.

- Lemon, which has a milder flavor than lime and contains sweet rose and fruity notes, cannot accentuate mango as nicely as lime.

- Check out the carousel to see an aide-memoire on mango flavor combinations

tips.title: BROWN BUTTER OR BEURRE NOISETTE
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

In the comments under yesterday's post, I noticed that for some people the technique of making brown butter was new and it raised questions and doubts.

Therefore, today I decided to share with you my tips and tricks in order to dispel your doubts and inspire you to make incredibly delicious blackberry, bilberry and star anise cupcakes while the berry season is in full swing.

Brown or browned butter (fr. beurre noisette) are all different names for the same product obtained by heating regular butter - it melts, separates into butterfat and milk solids, the latter sink to the bottom of the pan and turn a deep brown color.

The browning (caramelization) of butter is the result of the milk proteins and sugars going through the Maillard reaction upon heating to 130 °C.

The recipe for brown butter can be found in the previous post. But I’d like to give you some tips so that everything goes perfectly, and you don’t get nervous.

tips.title: 6 TIPS FOR GETTING THE PERFECT BEURRE NOISETTE
tips.docx:
1. Use a thick-bottomed saucepan to ensure even heating of the butter.

2. The saucepan should be of a light color - it’s more difficult to notice the change in the color of the butter against a dark background, and it can easily burn.

3. To get the perfect brown butter, I advise you to heat no more than 200 g of butter at a time in a small saucepan (d = 14-16 cm). If you need a larger amount, use a saucepan d = 22-26 cm.

4. When the butter gets frothy, start to constantly stir it with a whisk so that the milk solids do not burn.

5. After bringing the butter to 128 °C, remove the saucepan from the heat, while continuing to stir - within 30-40 seconds the residual heat of the saucepan will bring the butter to the desired slightly brownish color (it will heat up to 130-138 °C).

6. Immediately after this, pour the butter into a separate container to stop the cooking process. Otherwise, the temperature will continue to rise, and as soon as it exceeds 140 °C, the butter will burn.

tips.title: INFUSION. THE INS AND OUTS
tips.docx:
#marusya_infusion
part 1

At first glance, the topic is very simple and there is nothing to talk about. But! You will be surprised when you find out that even when I was giving a master class at a large-scale production, the guys were perplexed by my advice to change the method of infusion to cold.

In fact, aroma and taste are inextricably linked, and they should be considered as a whole.

You can read more about tastes and how they are created by the hashtag #marusya_flavours

Flavoring is an amazing thing that you encounter when diving into the world of confectionery. After baking ordinary shortbread cookies and charlotte, you get a bit bored and you feel a desire to play with new or unusual flavor combinations, add a subtle aroma.

The right aroma and taste of a dessert can calm a person or, on the contrary, energize, make them happy or make them think a little. For example, vanilla - brings warmth and tranquility, cinnamon - reminds of a warm autumn. Lemongrass and lavender have soothing effect.

In order to transfer the flavor of one ingredient to another, they must be combined under suitable conditions:

- mixed or blended together
- chilled together
- heated together
- boiled together

tips.title: WHAT CAN ONE INFUSE?
tips.docx:
In mousses:

- liquid base (cream/milk)
- syrup for cooking the egg whites (for Italian meringue-based mousse)
- mousses can also be flavored with pastes

- only thick pastes which don’t change, but rather improve the texture of the dessert, are used: nut, praline and some fruit pastes

In ganaches:

- fruit puree
- water

In berry fillings:

- berries or berry puree can undergo cold or vacuum infusion process

In sponges and other desserts that are baked at high temperatures:

- the flavoring is added directly to the composition of the product
part 2

In the previous part, we discussed with you what can be infused. Today I'll tell you about the most popular flavorings.

Most likely, the first thing that comes to mind is flavors. Both natural and artificial flavors will help to improve or change the taste of a dessert. This method is good for 3 reasons:

1. it doesn’t require much time and effort - add a drop, mix and it’s done!
2. it’s helpful when you don't want to add extra ingredients to the texture in order not to spoil it
3. it’s convenient if you need an unusual flavor (bubble gum, California strawberry, Tiramisu)

Apart from flavors, the following ingredients can be used to create an infusion:

### Vanilla (pod/paste/extract)

- Spices and seasoning (pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, anise, coriander, star anise, cloves, ginger)
- Herbs and flowers (tarragon, basil, dill, thyme, rosemary, lavender)
- Tea (black, matcha, red, green)
- Fruit pastes
- Citrus zest
- Freeze-dried berries
- Tonka beans
- Coffee beans
- Alcoholic drinks (rum, brandy, liqueurs)
- Syrups
- Natural essential extracts and oils

And this is not all!

Now let’s proceed to the most interesting part - infusion methods. They are:

- Hot
- Decoction
- Vacuum

tips.title: COLD METHOD
tips.docx:
Cold method consists in adding a certain flavor (spices, herbs, zest, etc.) to a liquid (cream, milk, berry puree), and then placing it in the fridge for at least 12 hours.

This is the longest method of infusion - the aromatization of the liquid occurs slowly and not as intensively as with the hot method.
It will take 3-5 days to almost completely extract flavor from fresh herbs into a liquid, and about 20 days for dry ones. In addition, a MORE flavoring component will be required.

But if you want to get an exquisite, sophisticated flavor and avoid heat treatment, this method will be the best option.

tips.title: FLAVOR PAIRING. APRICOT
tips.docx:
#marusya_flavor_pairing

People often ask me how I come up with all these ideas and sometimes just mind blowing flavor combinations. Should one be born with this ability or it’s possible to learn how to do it?

Answer: yes and no. Every creative skill can be seen as a double-edged sword.

On the one hand, it is natural aptitude, intuition and ability. On the other hand, it is knowledge. Behind any ability, be it the ability to create a new musical composition or a new cake, there is experience and a huge theoretical base, which have long been gained and, voluntarily or involuntarily, take part in the creation of a new masterpiece.

Creating new flavors, I, first of all, rely on my inner instinct. And no matter how much I want to, I can’t teach it. But along with my intuition, I also actively use knowledge from the science of combining ingredients - food pairing.

I’d love to share this particular knowledge. Therefore, today I am presenting a new series of posts on flavor pairing. And since the season of APRICOTS is now in full swing, let's talk about flavor combinations of this fruit first.

- sweet-tart
- a creamy, floral character
- a mixture of fresh notes of tropical fruits
- pronounced floral notes, in particular lavender

- fruity notes
- high concentration of creamy notes

Apricots match well with milky flavors as well as the floral components of other fruits. They perfectly pair with:

- other fruits such as peach, mango, raspberry, pear, mango, coconut. The most successful and striking combination is an apricot-raspberry pair.

- spices and seasoning - anise, ginger, cinnamon, vanilla, rosemary, zira, black pepper. Cardamom and apricot pair well in baked goods such as Danish apricot cookies or crumble, as well as jams.

- dairy products - goat cheese, cottage cheese, Greek yogurt
Pectin NH Nappage

There are plenty of articles about pectins, but this topic doesn’t seem to lose its relevance and the number of questions regarding this thickener and how to work with it is still huge:

- Why do I prefer pectin when I need to stabilize any berry or fruit filling?

- because pectin gives the most natural texture and, at the same time, it doesn’t affect the taste, smell and color of the finished product

- Why do I use pectin NH Nappage and not any other pectin, what’s special about it?

- pectin NH Nappage is used for the preparation of a neutral gel and glazes, as it allows to obtain a more transparent gel
- it’s thermoreversible - it can be reheated and frozen as many times as you need
- it doesn’t require a lot of sugar and / or acid in the mixture
- thanks to the presence of additional stabilizers in the composition, it perfectly stabilizes juices

- What is the composition of pectin NH Nappage, apart from E440 pectin itself?
- diphosphate E450 - stabilizer, acidity regulator, emulsifier, leavening agent, water-retaining agent
- calcium phosphate E341 - stabilizer, acidity regulator, leavening agent, color fixer
- dextrose - pure glucose - a monosaccharide, one hundred percent carbohydrate

- Which brands of pectin NH Nappage do I prefer?

### Spanish Sosa

- French Louis Francois

- How much pectin NH Nappage do you need to perfectly thicken the filling and how to introduce it correctly?

- the recommended dose is 0.8-2.0 g per 100 g of the mixture, depending on the content of pectin in the puree, the amount of water and the desired thickness of the filling
- pectin should be mixed with sugar in 1:5 ratio and then gradually sprinkled into the warm mixture. While doing it, stir the mixture constantly to avoid lumps
- it fully dissolves within 15 minutes

- Are there cases of pectin NH Nappage not setting the mixture?

- yes, this pectin practically doesn’t activate in mixtures containing alcohol

Which thickener do you prefer to use and why?

tips.title: CRÈME ANGLAISE FROM A TO Z
tips.docx:
As it turned out, not everyone can properly make the crème anglaise (French for "English cream") or custard. There’s nothing complicated about its preparation, but at the same time, to obtain a stable result, you need to follow a number of rules, as well as understand the processes that occur during its preparation.

So in order to avoid difficulties in working with the custard, you’ll need to know some tips and tricks which I’m going to share with you today.

Let's start with the concept of crème anglaise and custard.

Custard is a combination of water, fats and sugars which becomes possible thanks to an emulsifying agent.

Under normal conditions, fats and water don’t mix, but with the presence of an emulsifier it becomes possible.

Crème anglaise is a type of custard in which the emulsifying agent is the lecithin present in egg yolk.

Crème anglaise can be used as a standalone product, as well as a sauce (French version) or a base for making mousses, ice creams and creams (English version).

- Composition of crème anglaise:

- 70% - liquid (milk / milk + cream 1:1 / milk + fruit puree 1:1)
- 15% - egg yolks
- 15% - sugar

To make crème anglaise, mix egg yolks with sugar and boil the milk and/or cream. Pour 1/3 of milk into the yolk-sugar mixture, then pour everything back into a saucepan with the remaining milk. Bring to 82°C and remove from the stove.

Basically, you can use this recipe and get down to cooking. However, there’s a huge possibility that something will go wrong.

‼ To properly make crème anglaise, you should follow a number of rules:

- all ingredients must be fresh, as the enzymes contained in milk catalyze many biochemical processes
- all tools used to cook the custard must be perfectly clean
- use an appropriate tool at each stage of preparation: a whisk - for beating the yolks with sugar, a silicone spatula - for cooking the cream
- stick to the right temperatures - bring the cream to 82-83 °C to pasteurize it and obtain the desired consistency
part 2

I received an interesting question:

How can one cook crème anglaise to 82°C and not get an “omelette”?

To answer this question, let’s analyze the composition and properties of some ingredients that are used to make the custard.

### Yolk

Composition:

- 50-54% - water
- 30-33% - fats and lipids
- 16-17 - proteins (including lecithin)
- 1% - carbohydrates and minerals

It is thanks to lecithin that fats form an amalgam (emulsion) with a liquid. That is, an egg is, in fact, a natural emulsion.

‼ Lecithin must not be heated above 70°C

tips.title: Why Does Crème Anglaise Curdle? Reasons and Fixes
tips.docx:
Sugar
1. Sugar is very hygroscopic, that is, it has a high ability to absorb moisture.

I suggest doing a little experiment. Place one yolk in a bowl, add a couple of tbsp of sugar and leave it like that without stirring.

After a while, you’ll find that the mixture turned grainy - the sugar absorbed all the liquid from the yolk.

Therefore, when you start making crème anglaise, as soon as you add sugar to the yolks, IMMEDIATELY start to stir the mixture vigorously with a whisk! If during this process you decide to set it aside and answer a phone call, for example, the custard won’t be of the right texture anymore - the emulsion will break, which is IMPOSSIBLE TO FIX! If you continue to cook the custard using this mixture, you’ll get a lumpy mixture in your saucepan.

Next, we face another interesting task:

- As you remember, lecithin, which is found in the yolks, must not be heated above 70°C.

- But crème anglaise must be brought to 82-83°C in order to achieve the desired consistency and, most importantly, to pasteurize the product.

Here the 2nd property of sugar comes to the rescue:

2. Sugar prevents lecithin and proteins from overheating.

By adding sugar to the yolks, we thereby delay the destruction of lecithin, which allows us to bring the crème anglaise to 82°C and not cook it into an “omelette”.

- Even if you thoroughly stirred the yolks with sugar, there still is a risk of curdling (coagulation) of proteins.
part 3

As promised, today I’ll tell you why, when making crème anglaise, you still might cook it into an “omelette” after bringing it to 82 °C, even if you thoroughly whisked the sugar with yolks, protecting the lecithin from overheating.

The reason for this is quite obvious - the custard was brought to a higher temperature.

To measure the temperature correctly, follow guidelines:

- When cooking the custard, stir it with a spatula and not with a whisk to avoid air getting into the custard. When dealing with the aerated mixture it is almost impossible to measure the temperature correctly!

- Cooking crème anglaise with a whisk is considered a gross mistake!
- Firstly, you compromise the very concept of the custard by letting the air penetrate into it - thus you’ll get a mousse, not a custard.
- Secondly, you won’t be able to accurately measure the temperature of the mousse.

- Stir the custard carefully, making figure-eight motion with spatula - this will ensure uniform heating of the entire mixture and prevent it from scorching.

- Do not use a pyrometer to measure the temperature of the custard - it is designed to read the temperature on the surface! Use a probe thermometer istead, immersing it into the mixture (avoid touching the bottom of the pan!).

- However, if you are cooking on an induction stove, I do not recommend using a probe thermometer to check the temperature of the custard - no matter how hard you try, the device won’t read the temperature correctly, because:

- the bottom of the pans for induction stoves is metal, the probe is also metal, that is the induction heats it along with the pan - to put it another way, the probe thermometer will read not the temperature of the mixture, but the temperature the metal is heated to.

- Solution: If you have an induction stove, use a glass deep fry/candy thermometer
Part 4

Complete cooking instructions

1. Whisk the egg yolks and sugar.

- Whisk thoroughly and quickly to avoid lumps. You need to ensure a good emulsion so that the yolks don’t separate.

2. Heat the milk.

If you’re using pasteurized or UHT milk, bring it to 85°C.

If you’re using raw milk, bring it to a boil (100°C) to pasteurize.

- When the milk has boiled, a film forms on its surface - these are proteins that have coagulated. To prevent skin formation, add some sugar to the milk.
- It is best to use pasteurized dairy products to achieve a balanced taste in the final product.

3. Temper the egg yolks - gradually pour a third of the hot milk into the yolk mixture in a thin stream and mix well with a silicone spatula.

- If you pour the milk too quickly, the yolks can cook, while you only need to heat up the yolk mixture.

4. Pour in the remaining milk, put the saucepan on low heat and pasteurize the mixture at 82-83°C, stirring continuously with a spatula.

- Do not cook it on high heat - the custard may burn!

5. Remove the custard from the heat and pour it into a wide plastic vessel.

- If you used flavors (vanilla pod / zest / herbs), strain the custard first.

6. Place the vessel in a shock freezer or over an ice bath for quick cooling.

It is vital to quickly cool the custard to room temperature, as it is made from milk and eggs, which spoil quickly.

7. Cooled custard:

a) if you’re going to use crème anglaise as a standalone product or as a sauce, cover it with cling film in contact and place it in the fridge for further stabilization

b) if you’re going to use it as a base for frosting - add it to the remaining products (e.g. melted chocolate), cover with cling film in contact and place in the fridge

c) if you’re going to use it as a base for crémeux - first add melted gelatin mass, then quickly cool it, cover with cling film and place in the fridge
5 PROBLEMS WHEN MAKING CRÈME ANGLAISE AND HOW TO SOLVE THEM

This is a final post about crème anglaise, in which I’ll tell you what problems you may face in the process of making custard, and how to solve them.

1. Runny custard

Reason
The custard hasn’t been brought to 82-83 °C.

Crème anglaise contains the alpha-amylase enzyme which can break down protein.

If the custard has been brought to less than 74 °C, the alpha-amylase won't get destroyed and will digest the proteins. In other words, the custard will be runny. Such custard can't be fixed.

Solution
If the custard has been brought to a temperature above 75 °C, the product has been pasteurized (alpha-amylase is destroyed), it can be fixed - just add bloomed gelatin in order to make the custard more stable.

2. Custard has curdled

Reason
The custard was brought to a temperature above 82-83 °C.

Solution
In the future, be sure to measure the temperature correctly following the rules described in the previous post (P3). You can find them by the hashtag #marusya_about_crèmeanglaise

Someone advises blending curdled custard. Thus, you will eliminate the "lump effect", but won’t get rid of the omelette taste. Therefore, if your crème anglaise has split, I advise you to remake it so as not to compromise the whole cake.

3. Custard foams during cooking

Reason
See what’s in your hand. I'm sure it's a whisk.

Solution
After beating the yolks with sugar, put the whisk aside and switch to a silicone spatula. This is the appropriate tool to cook the custard with.

4. There are yolk pieces in custard

Reason
Poorly beaten yolks with sugar

Solution
Remake the custard

I don’t advise you to strain it. Yes, of course, you’ll get rid of pieces of yolk floating in the custard, but this won’t help you to get rid of the yolk taste.

5. Skin forms on the custard surface

Reason
The custard wasn’t covered with cling film or wasn't covered tightly enough.

Solution
Strain the custard or carefully remove the skin. Then cover the crème anglaise with cling film touching the surface.

json.title: Why Does Crème Anglaise Curdle? Reasons and Fixes
json.text:
Sugar
1. Sugar is very hygroscopic, that is, it has a high ability to absorb moisture.

I suggest doing a little experiment. Place one yolk in a bowl, add a couple of tbsp of sugar and leave it like that without stirring.

After a while, you’ll find that the mixture turned grainy - the sugar absorbed all the liquid from the yolk.

Therefore, when you start making crème anglaise, as soon as you add sugar to the yolks, IMMEDIATELY start to stir the mixture vigorously with a whisk! If during this process you decide to set it aside and answer a phone call, for example, the custard won’t be of the right texture anymore - the emulsion will break, which is IMPOSSIBLE TO FIX! If you continue to cook the custard using this mixture, you’ll get a lumpy mixture in your saucepan.

Next, we face another interesting task:

- As you remember, lecithin, which is found in the yolks, must not be heated above 70°C.

- But crème anglaise must be brought to 82-83°C in order to achieve the desired consistency and, most importantly, to pasteurize the product.

Here the 2nd property of sugar comes to the rescue:

2. Sugar prevents lecithin and proteins from overheating.

By adding sugar to the yolks, we thereby delay the destruction of lecithin, which allows us to bring the crème anglaise to 82°C and not cook it into an “omelette”.

- Even if you thoroughly stirred the yolks with sugar, there still is a risk of curdling (coagulation) of proteins.
part 3

As promised, today I’ll tell you why, when making crème anglaise, you still might cook it into an “omelette” after bringing it to 82 °C, even if you thoroughly whisked the sugar with yolks, protecting the lecithin from overheating.

The reason for this is quite obvious - the custard was brought to a higher temperature.

To measure the temperature correctly, follow guidelines:

- When cooking the custard, stir it with a spatula and not with a whisk to avoid air getting into the custard. When dealing with the aerated mixture it is almost impossible to measure the temperature correctly!

- Cooking crème anglaise with a whisk is considered a gross mistake!
- Firstly, you compromise the very concept of the custard by letting the air penetrate into it - thus you’ll get a mousse, not a custard.
- Secondly, you won’t be able to accurately measure the temperature of the mousse.

- Stir the custard carefully, making figure-eight motion with spatula - this will ensure uniform heating of the entire mixture and prevent it from scorching.

- Do not use a pyrometer to measure the temperature of the custard - it is designed to read the temperature on the surface! Use a probe thermometer istead, immersing it into the mixture (avoid touching the bottom of the pan!).

- However, if you are cooking on an induction stove, I do not recommend using a probe thermometer to check the temperature of the custard - no matter how hard you try, the device won’t read the temperature correctly, because:

- the bottom of the pans for induction stoves is metal, the probe is also metal, that is the induction heats it along with the pan - to put it another way, the probe thermometer will read not the temperature of the mixture, but the temperature the metal is heated to.

- Solution: If you have an induction stove, use a glass deep fry/candy thermometer

- When the milk has boiled, a film forms on its surface - these are proteins that have coagulated. To prevent skin formation, add some sugar to the milk.
- It is best to use pasteurized dairy products to achieve a balanced taste in the final product.

3. Temper the egg yolks - gradually pour a third of the hot milk into the yolk mixture in a thin stream and mix well with a silicone spatula.

- If you pour the milk too quickly, the yolks can cook, while you only need to heat up the yolk mixture.

4. Pour in the remaining milk, put the saucepan on low heat and pasteurize the mixture at 82-83°C, stirring continuously with a spatula.

- Do not cook it on high heat - the custard may burn!

tips.title: HOW TO DIFFERENTIATE VEGETABLE CREAM FROM DAIRY?
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

The previous post got more than 20 comments, so, as promised, I will tell you how to differentiate vegetable cream (or cream containing a mixture of non-dairy and dairy ingredients) from dairy cream at home.

Unfortunately, sometimes the name of the product or even its composition provided on the packaging is not really helpful in finding out whether it’s a dairy, vegetable or mixed imitation cream.

If you want to get quality pastry products with a rich taste, I advise you to carry out a small test before giving preference to a particular brand.

Put a small amount of cream in a saucepan and bring it to a boil.

- You’re dealing with vegetable / mixed imitation cream which contains a huge amount of thickeners and stabilizers, if after boiling it:

- has become even thicker than it was (sometimes it may look like low-fat sour cream)
- has not changed its original snow-white color

If you observe this with your cream, I can assume that it contains only vegetable fats or, at best, it has a mixed composition of milk and vegetable fats.

- You’re dealing with dairy cream, if after boiling it:

- has become liquid, the consistency resembles full-fat milk
- has acquired a yellowish tint, characteristic of dairy products (after heating, organic heavy cream acquires a well-defined milky or ivory color)

Similar processes are typical for cream of animal origin. You can trust a brand that has passed such a test.

I can share with you the brands that have passed this test in my kitchen.

The quality brands I trust:

- Mlekovita, 30/36%
- President, 33%
- Elle & Vire, 35%
- Debic, 32%

If you have read the post to the end, leave any emoji in the comments and bookmark the post

P.S. Be sure to test the origin of the cream you use. You'll get valuable experience in a matter of minutes!

tips.title: DAIRY AND NON-DAIRY WHIPPING CREAM
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

My students often ask me which cream is better to use.

First of all, I’d like to say that in my recipes I only use cream of animal origin. I don’t work with plant-based creams for a number of reasons:

- they contain a huge amount of stabilizers, flavors, preservatives and other synthetic components

- contain palm or palm kernel oil. During the preparation of vegetable cream, this oil is partially hydrogenated, that is, the liquid emulsion turns into solid fatty acids.

This is done for the sake of extending the expiration date to 12months. But at the same time, during hydrogenation trans fats are formed, which might affect our health:

- raise of cholesterol levels, negative effect on the immune and cardiovascular systems

- a higher risk of developing diabetes, liver, kidneys, heart and nervous system diseases. Trans fats have also been hypothesized to be carcinogenic.

- non-dairy cream cannot be heated as after that it may have an unpleasant taste. Such creams are usually used cold, which significantly narrows the range of their use in pastry

- and the last reason I don't work with vegetable cream is the low fat content

- The number one goal that I pursue when developing new recipes is to get the perfectly balanced taste. And these are the FAT MOLECULES that contribute to the FLAVOR! Therefore, I prefer to use dairy products with a high fat content.

It seems that to get the perfect dessert it is enough to pick any dairy cream in the supermarket and that's it. But it’s not! Unfortunately, quite often the information provided by manufacturers on packaging cannot be trusted, believe my own experience.

tips.title: HOW TO CHOOSE THE RIGHT CHOCOLATE FLUIDITY
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

Fluidity depends on the content of cocoa butter in chocolate - the more cocoa butter in its composition, the more fluid it is.

Chocolate with a higher fluidity contains more cocoa butter and when tempered properly, it allows you to create a hard, thin and crunchy chocolate coating with a glossy sheen.

Such chocolate contracts better during cooling, which makes it easier to remove the chocolate shell from the mold.

- Chocolate with a lower fluidity contains less cocoa butter, which produces a less hard, less shiny and thicker chocolate coating.

Determining the fluidity of chocolate is not difficult, as manufacturers indicate it on the packaging with a drop symbol system. The more drops are drawn on the packaging that you hold in your hands, the more fluid the chocolate is in front of you.

There is a wide range of fluidity levels marked with 1-5 drops:

- 1 drop
- ideal for mousse and frosting

- 2 drops
- perfect for making large molded chocolate figures

- 3 drops
- versatile chocolate suitable for making any texture: frosting, ganache for coating, icing, chocolates

- 4-5 drops
- ideal for molded chocolates with a thin chocolate shell

That is, depending on the application, you should choose a chocolate with the right fluidity.

In my work, I most often use milk or dark chocolate with a fluidity of 3 drops - its properties are most suitable for making ganaches for coating, crémeux, as well as mousse and baked chocolate cheesecakes.

tips.title: SEVERAL THICKENERS IN A FILLING. WHY?
tips.docx:
In online courses and during live master classes, which I miss so much, students often ask me why they need to add gelatin if they have already added pectin to the preparation.

The question is really good and very interesting. Let’s find the answer now!

The thing is that each thickener has different properties:

### Agar-agar

- gives a delicate, "glassy", not elastic texture
- activates at high temperatures (90-100°C). If added to a cold mixture, it starts to set at 40°C and form lumps
- must not be frozen as it may lose its properties
- if you process the gelled mixture with a blender, you’ll get a gel

### Gelatin

- gives good elasticity and makes the fillings a bit “rubbery”
- activates at low temperatures (can be added at 25-30°C)
- retains its properties when frozen
- it takes at least 6-7 hours for the filling to set
- contains a large amount of protein, which allows one to whip it and get a thick foam

### Pectin (NH, NH Nappage)

- gives a stable, jam-like texture and doesn’t affect the taste of the mixture
- activates at high temperatures (80-100°C)
- retains its properties when frozen
- fillings made with pectin can be reheated

Sometimes when we want our filling to get the properties of 2 different thickeners at once, we add gelatin or agar-agar to the pectin.

For example, when making the Kiwi-Lime-Bergamot cheesecake, the photo of which you can see in the carousel, I used both pectin (to give light elasticity and natural taste) and agar-agar (for stability) to prepare the Mojito marmalade made from vermouth, lime juice and bergamot.

In this case, the gelatin can’t be used to stabilize (gel) the mixture. Can you guess why?
