tips.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE
tips.docx:
Personally, I prefer the hot infusion, since it is much more effective and does not require such a long preparation.

The hot method suggests heating the whipping cream / milk with flavoring up to 90 °C / 194 °F over low heat. Then you should cover the mixture with a lid and let it infuse for at least 2-3 hours. For an intense flavor, you may repeat the process one more time.

If you use flowers, leaves, coffee grains, tonka beans or tea as a flavoring, it’s a good idea to process the whipping cream together with the flavoring with a blender before heating.

But in this case you should increase the amount of whipping cream / milk by 30-40%, and after infusion simply strain the mass through a strainer or a piece of cheesecloth.

ℹOnly a metal cake pan with a removable bottom is good for baking cheesecake.

At first glance, this is a correct statement, because in this case unmolding the cheesecake can be done with your eyes shut. In fact, cheesecakes can be baked equally well in cake pans with removable bottom and in baking rings.

Just when dealing with baking rings, beginners will immediately face two seemingly difficult tasks:

- how to shape and then transfer a cheesecake in a baking ring without a bottom, because after baking the dessert is unstable and requires careful treatment.

There are several solutions to this problem.

In order to easily transfer the cheesecake to the oven and then to the fridge, you can place the baking ring on the bottom of the old split cake mold of a slightly larger diameter, covered with a sheet of parchment paper.

I use another method - I wrap the bottom of the baking ring in several layers of foil and put it on a thick cake base.

You can, of course, put the ring directly on the baking sheet, provided that its surface is perfectly flat, but in this case you will not be able to use it until the cheesecake is completely cooled. To be continued.

- how to unmold a seemingly glued cheesecake from a baking ring without destroying its ideal shape.

Firstly, remember to apply a thin layer of oil (I prefer coconut oil) on the baking ring and unmold the cheesecake out only after 6 hours of cooling.

Secondly, if you leave a cheesecake at room temperature for 15-20 minutes, the oil will slightly melt and you will only need to carefully lift the baking ring up. The cheesecake will remain on the cake base.

- Useful tips:

- To speed up the process of unmolding the cheese, you may heat the baking ring up with a heat gun or a hair dryer.

- Preferably, the cheesecake should not be higher than 6 cm (without décor).

- Try to shape the sides of the shortbread shell so that the cheese mass is only slightly below the level of the sides, otherwise it may detach slightly after baking.

ℹCheesecake must be baked at low temperatures (not higher than 120 °C / 248 °F) with a water bath.

Let me remind you that a water bath is a baking sheet full of boiling water installed on the lowest level of the oven.

Please, pay your attention to the fact that you should not pour water into the baking sheet with the cheesecake, otherwise the water will get into the mold and your cheesecake will get wet.
In fact, the baking mode for a cheesecake depends on the characteristics of your oven. Cheesecakes can be baked at either 90-100 °C / 194-212 °F or 150-160 °C / 302-320 °F, with or without a water bath.

If you bake your cheesecake at a very low temperature (90-100 °C / 194-212 °F), then you probably won't need a water bath. But if your oven is so powerful that even at 90 °C / 194 °F the cheesecake rises and its top burns - put a water bath - it lowers the heat in the oven.

I used to bake cheesecakes with a water bath and strictly at a temperature not more than 120 °C / 248 °F. It would take my cheesecakes at least 3-4 hours to bake, and for a long time I could not understand what I was doing wrong.

Then a brilliant idea came across my mind and I bought a thermometer for the oven. It turned out that my 120 °C / 248 °F + a water bath = 80-90 °C / 176-194 °F of real temperature. Now, when baking a cheesecake with a water bath, I set the temperature to at least 150 °C / 302 °F and my thermometer shows exactly 120 °C / 248 °F. The cheesecake is ready in 1.5 hours!

ℹYou can bake cheesecakes using absolutely any oven mode.

It all depends on the situation, and, again, on the characteristics of your oven. If the top heating element heats too much, then turn on only the bottom one. In 80% of cases, conventional heating is the best option. If you need to bake several trays at the same time, use the convection mode.

If you have difficulties with the baking mode and the uniformity of baking, you can cover the top of the cheesecake with foil. This will keep the light color of the cheesecake and prevent it from being burnt.

- Add the flavouring directly to the cheese mass.

- What could it be?

- berry, fruit purees
- whole berries and fruit pieces
- caramel, dulce de leche
- chocolate, ganache, Nutella
- nuts and nut paste
- instant coffee, matcha tea
- liqueurs, cognac and other alcoholic beverages.

You need to work very carefully, since each of these flavourings has a different water and sugar content. The most important advice I want to give is that berry or fruit purees should be pre-thickened with cornstarch.

Add the starch to the puree and constantly stirring bring it to a boil - you should get a thick mass. It is also possible to go without pre-cooking, but then the texture of the cheesecake will be a little softer.

If you add alcohol, then reduce the cream / milk in the recipe by the same amount, if you do not want the cheesecake to be very tender.

- Infuse cream or milk.

- You may infuse it with:

- cinnamon stick, vanilla pod, saffron, whole star anise, cardamom, or any other spice
- lavender and violets flowers, rose petals
- leaves of mint, lemon balm, basil, thyme
- coffee beans
- tonka beans
- lemon, orange or lime zest
- green, black, milk or any other tea
- blue cheeses and more.

There are two ways of infusion- cold and hot one.

As for the cold method, it is enough to add flavoring to the cream / milk and leave it overnight, or even better for a day, in the fridge.

json.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE
json.text:
ℹ If you open the oven, the cheesecake will collapse.

Stupidity! The cheesecake shouldn't rise at all. If it rises, it means that the temperature that you set for it is too high.

ℹ Never open the oven while the cheesecake is baking.

Also wrong. If the cheesecake is baking at low temperatures, then nothing bad will happen if you open the oven.

ℹ On average, any cheesecake should be baked for at least 1.5-2.0 hours.

In fact, the baking time will depend on many factors — the characteristics of your oven, the temperature you set (90-150 °C / 194-302 °F), the height of the cheesecake (4-6 cm), taste (chocolate, caramel, berry or fruit), and also the number of cheesecakes (two cheesecakes in the oven will bake 20-30 minutes longer, for example).

That's why there is only one way out — to check its readiness using a piece of advice from the next paragraph. Usually, a cheesecake with a diameter of 16-18 cm and a height of 5-6 cm is baked for about 100 minutes.

ℹ How to check the doneness of a cheesecake?

By touching the cheesecake’s top with your finger. It should remain clean, while the middle of the cheese should slightly jiggle, like jelly.

- Do not worry if some butter leaks onto the baking tray during baking. You used it to grease the ring, and it’s natural that it melts at high temperatures. It doesn’t affect the texture and taste of the base at all.

- Turn off the oven, slightly open the door and leave the cheesecake to cool down inside for about 30-40 minutes. Then take the cheesecake out of the oven and leave it at room temperature until it cools down completely. After that, put it in the fridge for 6-12 hours.

- If you put a still warm cheesecake in the fridge, the condensation may form and the base will soak from moisture.

- Coat the cheesecake with a variety of fillings and décor only after it has completely cooled down (at least 6 hours).

Now there are only a few questions left to deal with:

ℹ What can be used to decorate the cheesecake?

- fresh berries, fruits
- coulis, confit, berry / fruit sauces, jellies, etc., in short, everything that can be made from fruits / berries and their puree with the addition of a thickener
- regular or whipped ganache
- regular or whipped caramel
- nuts, meringue, creams, namelaka, cremeux, gels, glazes, etc.

ℹ How long does a cheesecake last?

The shelf life of any product depends on the way it was made, the products used in it and the storage temperature. That’s why the only thing that I can say is that on average, the shelf life of baked cheesecakes is no more than 3-4 days in the fridge. Then, how long you will be able to resist this sweet temptation is up to you.

ℹ Can cheesecakes be frozen?

If it is dry and there are no foreign odors in the freezer, you can freeze a cheesecake and store it for not more than 20-30 days.

- I don't advise freezing cheesecakes if you are unsure about your freezer, but if you need to freeze a cheesecake without a cake base, make sure to wrap it in plastic wrap.

- You can turn any large cheesecake into individual cakes, and vice versa. Just keep in mind that the baking time will change. For individual cheesecakes it’s 50-60 minutes maximum at the temperature that is 10-20 °C / 50-68 °F lower than usual.

ℹ What texture does a perfect cheesecake have?

It’s like with zefir – everyone has their own preferences. First of all, YOU should like the cheesecake! It all depends solely on your taste and nothing else!

tips.title: PERFECT BORDERS
tips.docx:
Perhaps the most difficult thing in the process of baking cheesecakes is to achieve perfectly beautiful borders, both externally and in the cut.

For sure, the even borders take your cheesecake from the category of an ordinary homemade pastry to the rank of a culinary masterpiece, don’t they?

By the way, how are you doing with the borders? Are you satisfied with your result?

At the very beginning, when I baked my first cheese cakes, making a crust was the most lengthy and painful moment of the whole process.

I tried almost all the tools! Glasses, mugs, spoons, dough scrapers - I've tested everything! I used to spend at least 40-50 minutes for one cheese cake. There was even a period when I awaited this moment with horror and panic.

But hard work and experience overcame everything. Six months later, the perfect base was ready in 15 minutes using a spoon as an improvised tool.

Now I form an ideal crust in 4-5 minutes, sometimes with only my bare hands staying absolutely calm.

What's the secret, you ask? Is it just a vast experience?

Not really. The secret of a quick and perfect base for a cheesecake is a good recipe and the right technique. Well, experience, of course, will come in handy

A few tips and tricks for you:

- reconstituted shortbread should shape well and keep its shape when squeezed, while remaining crumbly

- both butter and coconut oil can be used to change the structure the shortbread

- in the latter case, the base will be more crumbly and crunchy, and it will also be much more easier to unmold it

- forming the base of the cheesecake, try to distribute the crumbs along the bottom and sides in an even layer

- pay attention to the fact that the thickness of the crust from bottom to top should be the same

- also make sure that a thick layer of dough does not form between the bottom and the borders

- in order to avoid the latter, first completely form the borders, and only then proceed to the bottom

json.title: PERFECT BORDERS
json.text:
Perhaps the most difficult thing in the process of baking cheesecakes is to achieve perfectly beautiful borders, both externally and in the cut.

For sure, the even borders take your cheesecake from the category of an ordinary homemade pastry to the rank of a culinary masterpiece, don’t they?

By the way, how are you doing with the borders? Are you satisfied with your result?

At the very beginning, when I baked my first cheese cakes, making a crust was the most lengthy and painful moment of the whole process.

I tried almost all the tools! Glasses, mugs, spoons, dough scrapers - I've tested everything! I used to spend at least 40-50 minutes for one cheese cake. There was even a period when I awaited this moment with horror and panic.

But hard work and experience overcame everything. Six months later, the perfect base was ready in 15 minutes using a spoon as an improvised tool.

Now I form an ideal crust in 4-5 minutes, sometimes with only my bare hands staying absolutely calm.

What's the secret, you ask? Is it just a vast experience?

Not really. The secret of a quick and perfect base for a cheesecake is a good recipe and the right technique. Well, experience, of course, will come in handy

A few tips and tricks for you:

- reconstituted shortbread should shape well and keep its shape when squeezed, while remaining crumbly

- both butter and coconut oil can be used to change the structure the shortbread

- in the latter case, the base will be more crumbly and crunchy, and it will also be much more easier to unmold it

- forming the base of the cheesecake, try to distribute the crumbs along the bottom and sides in an even layer

- pay attention to the fact that the thickness of the crust from bottom to top should be the same

- also make sure that a thick layer of dough does not form between the bottom and the borders

- in order to avoid the latter, first completely form the borders, and only then proceed to the bottom

tips.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE
tips.docx:
I am glad that you find the tips on making the perfect cheesecake useful, so I will be happy to continue. If you like this idea, leave + in the comments!

ℹIs it necessary to use room temperature ingredients to make the cheese filling?

No, it won’t affect the taste, the texture or the look of the pastry in any way. In fact, only the temperature of the cream cheese matters, because when the cream cheese is at room temperature, it is much softer and then it’s easier to mix the mass until smooth, avoiding lumps.

Useful tip:

- If you forgot to get the cream cheese out of the fridge beforehand, you may slightly heat it up over a water bath or in the microwave oven.

ℹDo not whip the mass for a long time, otherwise there might be cracks on the surface of the cheesecake due to the excess of air in the mass. Work at low speed.

In fact, it is enough to understand that the cheesecake should be mixed until smooth, and not whipped until fluffy.

As for the cracks that appear due to air bubbles, I'm sure this is more of a myth. There were several cases when I used cold cream cheese and overwhipped the cheese mass trying to get rid of the lumps. There were bubbles, but no cracks.

The reason for the formation of cracks on the surface of the cheesecake is actually very simple - the baking temperature is too high, but I will write about it in detail later in the article.

- Useful tip:

It is better to introduce the eggs into the cheese filling one at a time, each time mixing the mass until smooth.

json.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE
json.text:
ℹ If you open the oven, the cheesecake will collapse.

Stupidity! The cheesecake shouldn't rise at all. If it rises, it means that the temperature that you set for it is too high.

ℹ Never open the oven while the cheesecake is baking.

Also wrong. If the cheesecake is baking at low temperatures, then nothing bad will happen if you open the oven.

ℹ On average, any cheesecake should be baked for at least 1.5-2.0 hours.

In fact, the baking time will depend on many factors — the characteristics of your oven, the temperature you set (90-150 °C / 194-302 °F), the height of the cheesecake (4-6 cm), taste (chocolate, caramel, berry or fruit), and also the number of cheesecakes (two cheesecakes in the oven will bake 20-30 minutes longer, for example).

That's why there is only one way out — to check its readiness using a piece of advice from the next paragraph. Usually, a cheesecake with a diameter of 16-18 cm and a height of 5-6 cm is baked for about 100 minutes.

ℹ How to check the doneness of a cheesecake?

By touching the cheesecake’s top with your finger. It should remain clean, while the middle of the cheese should slightly jiggle, like jelly.

- Do not worry if some butter leaks onto the baking tray during baking. You used it to grease the ring, and it’s natural that it melts at high temperatures. It doesn’t affect the texture and taste of the base at all.

- Turn off the oven, slightly open the door and leave the cheesecake to cool down inside for about 30-40 minutes. Then take the cheesecake out of the oven and leave it at room temperature until it cools down completely. After that, put it in the fridge for 6-12 hours.

- If you put a still warm cheesecake in the fridge, the condensation may form and the base will soak from moisture.

- Coat the cheesecake with a variety of fillings and décor only after it has completely cooled down (at least 6 hours).

Now there are only a few questions left to deal with:

ℹ What can be used to decorate the cheesecake?

- fresh berries, fruits
- coulis, confit, berry / fruit sauces, jellies, etc., in short, everything that can be made from fruits / berries and their puree with the addition of a thickener
- regular or whipped ganache
- regular or whipped caramel
- nuts, meringue, creams, namelaka, cremeux, gels, glazes, etc.

ℹ How long does a cheesecake last?

The shelf life of any product depends on the way it was made, the products used in it and the storage temperature. That’s why the only thing that I can say is that on average, the shelf life of baked cheesecakes is no more than 3-4 days in the fridge. Then, how long you will be able to resist this sweet temptation is up to you.

ℹ Can cheesecakes be frozen?

If it is dry and there are no foreign odors in the freezer, you can freeze a cheesecake and store it for not more than 20-30 days.

- I don't advise freezing cheesecakes if you are unsure about your freezer, but if you need to freeze a cheesecake without a cake base, make sure to wrap it in plastic wrap.

- You can turn any large cheesecake into individual cakes, and vice versa. Just keep in mind that the baking time will change. For individual cheesecakes it’s 50-60 minutes maximum at the temperature that is 10-20 °C / 50-68 °F lower than usual.

ℹ What texture does a perfect cheesecake have?

It’s like with zefir – everyone has their own preferences. First of all, YOU should like the cheesecake! It all depends solely on your taste and nothing else!

tips.title: WATER BATH AND CHEESECAKE
tips.docx:
One of the questions that I receive quite often from people who bought the cheesecake recipe concerns the water bath: what’s that? Where should I pour the water?

I'm wondering, without reading the post, what are your ideas? Write them in the comments section, please! I will read your answers with pleasure.

Done? Great! Now let's figure out how the cheesecake should be baked.

In fact, you may bake a cheesecake both over a water bath and in a water bath, or even without using water at all. So, what is the water bath in cooking in general and how is it better to bake a cheesecake - over or in the water bath?

- A water bath is a method of cooking, in which the liquid is heated without direct contact of the container with fire. This method is used when the required temperature of the mass that is being cooked should not exceed 100 °C / 212 °F.

- Cooking over a water bath suggests pouring the water into the lower bowl or container, and placing the product, which will be cooked over a water bath, in the upper one. In this case, the height of the upper bowl should be smaller in order to leave room for boiling water. Moreover, the water in the larger bowl should not boil too much. This construction is usually used for cooking on the stove.

- Cooking in a water bath suggests placing a small bowl directly into a larger container, into which the hot water is poured. The level of water should reach the middle of the inner bowl. This construction is often used for baking in the oven.

When baking over the water bath, the cheesecake is placed on a baking sheet / wire rack at the top of the oven, while the second baking sheet or any other container filled with hot water is placed at the bottom.

When baking in the water bath, the cheesecake pan is placed directly into a large container filled with hot water.

I do not recommend baking the cheesecake in the water bath, as there is a high chance of water getting into the mold resulting in a wet base of the cheesecake!

I suggest paying closer attention to this popular American dessert and trying to figure out together which rules for its preparation should be considered as indisputable facts, and which can be neglected.

Let’s bust the myths! And I’ll start with making the shortbread crust.

- It is very convenient to use a flat bottom mug (not the one with the concave bottom) with sides at right angle for forming the cheesecake base. Also, a tablespoon might be quite helpful.

- If after baking the sides of the shortbread crust have slid down, replace the butter with a thicker one and try to use less of it.

- It is much easier and faster not to bake the formed shortbread crust, but simply put it in the freezer for 30-60 minutes.

- If you use the coconut oil instead of butter for the reconstituted shortbread crust, the base will come out crispier and crumblier, and it will be easier to unmold it.

tips.title: Stabilizing Whipped Cream
tips.docx:
- In warm weather, adding gelatin or a stabilizer to heavy whipped cream can be beneficial for maintaining its shape.

- This is especially important for dishes featuring heavy whipped cream that will be displayed or served on a buffet table. Don’t forget to hit and save this post so you can easily refer to it when needed.

How to Use a Stabilizer
Sift the stabilizer along with the powdered sugar you’ll use to sweeten the heavy whipped cream.

- Use approximately 7 g of stabilizer per liter of heavy whipped cream, or follow the package instructions. Add the sugar and stabilizer during the whipping process.

Gelatin Method
For gelatin, use the following proportions:

▫ 1 liter of heavy whipped cream
▫ 10 g of gelatin
▫ 60 ml of cold water

- Soak the gelatin in cold water, then heat it until fully dissolved. Whip the cream until it begins to thicken, then gradually and evenly pour in the gelatin while continuing to whip to the desired consistency.

tips.title: How to Make Perfect Chocolate Drips
tips.docx:
#marusya_theory_tips

Chocolate drips are an elegant and seemingly simple decoration for a cake, in fact, they also require certain knowledge and skills.

Today we decided to reveal all the secrets, so grab your pens and notepads, and get ready to be all ears!

Step 1. Dark Chocolate Drip Icing
You will need:

- 75 g dark chocolate 54.5%
- 25 g of odorless vegetable oil
- heat-resistant silicone spatula
- plastic bowl

While stirring, melt the chocolate over a water bath or in pulses in the microwave oven, add the vegetable oil and mix thoroughly until completely smooth.
▪ melt the chocolate in short pulses, 5–8 seconds, stirring vigorously with a spatula after each pulse
▪ do not overheat the chocolate, otherwise it will curdle – for dark chocolate, the maximum temperature is 50–55 °C
▪before applying to the cake, the temperature of the icing should be 32–34 °C – if it is slightly higher or lower, you’ll get either thick and rough drips (the icing isn’t warm enough) or very thin translucent drips (overheated icing)

Step 2. Applying the Drips
You will need:

- pastry bag
- scissors
- offset spatula

Pour the chocolate icing into a piping bag and make a small cut. Pipe the slightly warm icing on the edge of the chilled cake, allowing some of the icing to roll off the edge and run down the side. Pour the rest of the icing into the center of the cake and spread it over with an offset spatula.
▪to get neat drips, it’s more convenient to use a pastry bag rather than a spoon – you’ll be able to adjust the thickness of the drips by making a cut bigger
▪ the cake should be well chilled as the cold surface slows down the drips, preventing them from running down the entire length of the cake
▪apply drips at the same distance from each other, but make them of different length, adjusting it with the amount of icing piped out

tips.title: Basic Savory Crumble
tips.docx:
- 90 g butter 82%
- 20 g icing sugar
- 40 g whole eggs (~0.7 pcs)
- 150 g all-purpose flour
- 10 g cornstarch
- 40 g ground hazelnuts/almonds
- 3 g salt

- Combine softened butter and icing sugar until well mixed. Add the egg melange and mix again. Incorporate sifted flour and cornstarch, ground nuts, and salt. Mix everything with a mixer for 30–40 seconds until crumbly. Be cautious not to overmix the dough.

- Transfer the shortcrust crumbs onto a baking sheet lined with parchment paper, spread them evenly, and place in the freezer for at least 30 minutes. Bake in a preheated oven at 170–180 °C for approximately 15–20 minutes. Allow the crumble to cool completely. The baked shortcrust crumble should be crisp and golden.

The basic savory crumble is now ready!

- to form the cheesecake crust with savory crumble, I typically incorporate some ground nuts, spices to taste, around 20–30 g of milk, 20 g of butter, and 15 g of coconut oil into the baked shortcrust crumble

Swipe through the carousel and enjoy enticing photos of savory cheesecakes — Philadelphia, Marseille, and, of course, Crepes with Red Caviar

tips.title: FLAVOR PAIRING. STRAWBERRY
tips.docx:
#marusya_flavor_pairing

Each of us is familiar with the taste of bright, juicy strawberries disturbing our imagination and appetite. But do we know everything about its aroma profile? What will it pair well with?

Let's do a foodpairing autopsy of the favorite of millions

### Flavor Description
▪ sweet "candy"
▪ nice acidity
▪ top fruity notes
▪ light creamy aftertaste
▪ caramel notes
▪ inherent oiliness

Strawberries can be leading — then you need weaker flavors that emphasize the intensity of its taste, sweetness. If strawberries are as addition, beat the leading flavor with spices or heat treatment.

### Aroma Profile
▪ fruity aroma
▪ sweet caramel notes
▪ light grassiness
▪ spicy notes of vanilla
▪ strong resemblance to tomato aromatics

The aroma profile of strawberries is composed of over 360 components, including esters, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, terpenes, furanones, and sulfur compounds. The aroma of ripe strawberries is recognized as one of the most complex fruit flavors.

Pairs well with:

- nuts — almonds, cashews, pistachios and pecans. The ideal nutty companion — hazelnuts — does not overlap the taste of strawberries, but gently complements it.

- other fruits and berries such as orange, pineapple, melon, raspberry, coconut

The flavor combination strawberry-tomato deserves special attention — the natural flavor of strawberries is very similar to the aromatics of tomatoes, so the presence of tomatoes in dessert tarts, stracciatella and bruschettas is increasingly being traced

- spices, herbs and seasonings — vanilla, cinnamon, mint, ginger, lemongrass and... balsamic vinegar! Just a couple of drops of balsamic can greatly enhance the taste of strawberries. The combination is often used by chefs in salads, tarts.

- dairy products – cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, cream, mascarpone, cream cheese
- Strawberry-Soft Cheeses — strawberries have soft, creamy, buttery notes in their flavor, making them a great partner for soft milk, creamy, cheeses and cottage cheese.

json.title: Preparing frostings
json.text:
I constantly remind my students that making frosting is a process inseparable from assembling the cake.

All whipped (aerated) frostings — buttercream, ganache, sour-cream or cream-cheese frosting — must be used right after preparation.

 They cannot be stored and shouldn’t be prepared in advance.

Butter-based frostings can be kept in the fridge at 2–6°C (~35–43°F) for no more than 5 hours.

- Storing finished products that contain frostings

The container must be clean, dry, and free of foreign odors.

All baked goods must be stored in the fridge at 2–6°C (~35–43°F) after being made.

The shelf life of frostings depends on their composition (eggs, alcohol, purées, fat content of dairy products, etc.) and storage conditions (room-temp display, fridge, and how often it is opened).

Buttercream frosting: 24 to 72 hours depending on ingredients (24 hours if eggs, like “Charlotte”).

Buttercream can be frozen for up to 1 month.

Meringue frosting: up to 72 hours in the fridge, up to 12 hours at room temp (~20–22°C/~68–72°F).

Custard-based frosting: at 4–6°C (~39–43°F) it keeps 48–72 hours (2–3 days). At room temp (~23–50°C/~73–122°F) only 6–12 hours because it spoils quickly. Cool quickly to 4°C (~39°F) after cooking to prevent bacterial growth, especially in the 23–50°C (~73–122°F) range.

Sour-cream frosting: in the fridge 4–6°C (~39–43°F) - 12–36 hours depending on fat content and ingredients. At room temp (~23–50°C/~73–122°F) - up to 6 hours. If used in cakes, keeps up to 3 days in the fridge at 4–6°C (~39–43°F).

Cream-based frosting: depends on ingredients and preparation method. Cream-cheese, sour-cream-and-cream, and butter-and-cream frostings keep up to 36 hours in the fridge at 4–6°C (~39–43°F).

Cheesecake-style or cream-cheese frosting: up to 48 hours in the fridge at 4–6°C (~39–43°F). Cream cheese should not sit at room temp (~23–50°C/~73–122°F) for more than 2 hours.

Ganache: depending on composition, from 72 hours in the fridge 4–6°C (~39–43°F) to several months at room temp (~23–50°C/~73–122°F).
Mascarpone vs. Cream Cheese: Key Differences

Despite their similarities and wide use in cooking, mascarpone and cream cheese differ in production methods, composition, and properties.

Understanding these differences helps you choose the right product each time and substitute it when needed.

Mascarpone

json.title: Origin: traditional Italian cheese
json.text:
- Fat content: 70–75%, almost as rich as butter
- Flavor and aroma: delicate, creamy, with a buttery note; almost neutral, enhancing other flavors harmoniously
- Texture: very soft, silky, prone to separating if overwhipped
- Production: typically made by adding acid to warmed heavy cream. The combination of acid and heat coagulates the casein, forming a fine, smooth cheese mass
- Uses: classic ingredient in tiramisu; used in mousses, creams, and desserts where high fat content and velvety texture are desired

Cream Cheese

- Origin: industrially developed product, common in the US and Europe
- Fat content: on average 30–35%
- Flavor and aroma: mild with noticeable tang and slight saltiness, which helps balance the sweetness in desserts
- Texture: denser and more stable compared to mascarpone
- Production: made by adding lactic acid bacteria and often enzymes to milk or cream. Once the liquid whey is drained, the cheese is processed until it reaches the desired consistency
- Uses: base for cheesecakes, frostings, and fillings; provides structure and holds its shape well

Mascarpone offers a rich flavor, creaminess, and a buttery texture, but is less stable during processing.

Cream cheese ensures density and structure, adds a light tang that balances sweetness, but is less intensely creamy.

To sum up, the choice depends on the desired result:
• Mascarpone is ideal for delicate frostings and mousse-based desserts
• Cream cheese is best for recipes where stability, shape, and flavor balance are important

json.title: Baking soda
json.text:
Why baking soda ≠ baking powder?

And how to know which one you need for what you’re baking?

Works only in combination with an acid—kefir, lemon juice, honey, etc.

The reaction starts immediately as soon as the ingredients are combined. Carbon dioxide begins to release, so the dough must go straight into the oven. If you wait too long, the baked goods won’t rise properly.

json.title: Baking powder
json.text:
It’s a combination of baking soda and a dry acid.

It comes in several forms, the most common being double-acting. Baked goods made with double-acting baking powder need heat to fully activate the leavening. A small amount of carbon dioxide is released when mixing; the rest is released during baking. This removes the need for rushing to portion and bake to ensure the dough rises just as good.

json.title: Ammonium (ammonium carbonate)
json.text:
Lesser known, but a very effective leavening agent.

Perfect for thin and dry baked goods— various cookies, including gingerbread cookies, wafers. Gives incredible crispness and lightness. However, it’s not used in large cakes or loaves: the smell of ammonia can stay in the finished product.

json.title: Substitution
json.text:
•Baking soda for baking powder—1 : 3 or triple the amount of baking powder.

•Baking powder for baking soda—3 : 1 or use 1 part soda + 2 parts cream of tartar for every 3 parts baking powder.

- So if you’re making sponges or cakes with acidic ingredients, you can use baking soda.

- If you need more control and stability—choose baking powder or a combo of soda + baking powder.

- For thin crispy cookies or gingerbread dough—ammonium will be your secret ingredient.

json.title: Temperature
json.text:
Egg whites straight from the fridge don’t whip well.
The ideal temperature for whipping is room temperature, around 21 °C (~70°F).

Warm egg whites capture air better, foam faster, and create a more stable structure.

- Density of egg whites (freshness)

Runny (older) whites are easy to whip, give more volume,
- but the foam is less stable and collapses quickly.
Fresh whites are thicker, and harder to whip,
- but the foam structure is strong and stable.

- If volume is important—it’s better to use older eggs.
- If you need stability—choose fresh ones, and leave the older whites for regular baking.

json.title: Whipping time
json.text:
Both extremes—underwhipping and overwhipping—hurt meringue stability.

⏩Underwhipped whites—proteins don’t aggregate enough to form a solid film.
This kind of foam is unstable and spreads quickly.
⏩Overwhipped whites—with too long or aggressive whipping, the proteins denature and over-aggregate. The film around each air bubble becomes overstretched and loses elasticity.

In other words, overwhipping has a curdling/separating effect on the egg white structure, similar to overheating.
The result is tightly bound, inelastic clumps of protein sitting in expelled liquid. This mass is no longer usable—you’ll have to throw it away.

json.title: Other factors
json.text:
⏩Salt
Decreases foam stability. It shouldn’t be added during whipping.

⏩Whisk type
Thick wires—create large bubbles, less stable foam.
Thin whisk—creates small, uniform bubbles, more stable foam.

json.title: Moisturizers
json.text:
Ingredients like water, milk, syrups, and eggs provide moisture.

Interestingly, some ingredients serve multiple functions. You didn’t think it was all so straightforward, did you?

If a cake is too dry, increasing the amount of moisturizers can help. However, be cautious, as most ingredients have multiple roles. For example, adding more eggs to a dry cake could result in an even drier and tougher texture.

json.title: Dryers
json.text:
Ingredients such as flour, starch, and cocoa absorb moisture.

The idea of a well-balanced recipe formula lies in the proportionate amounts of stabilizers that will balance out the softeners and dryers that will balance out the moisturizers. For instance, increasing stabilizers requires a corresponding increase in softeners.
Have been delving into the theory of flour for a while.

I have known about the power and importance of gluten (protein) for quite some time. But this time it’s a completely different level.

In nutshell. In addition to protein (~12%), the main part of flour is starch (~71%).

On which type of wheat for making flour is used (hard or soft kernel) will depend not only the quantity and quality of protein, the texture of the flour, but also the number of broken and damaged starch granules.

That is, the harder the wheat kernel, the more difficult it is to grind it into fine flour and the more starch granules will be damaged in the process.

And damaged starch granules absorb much more water than intact ones, which slows staling.

Damaged granules are also more susceptible than intact ones to breakdown down by amylase, which further slows staling.

In addition, as the amylase breaks down starches into sugars, yeast fermentation can increase.

That’s why flour for bread is milled from hard red wheat, which not only has a high protein content, but also many damaged starch granules.

Bread flours are typically used for pan breads, rolls, croissants and sweet yeast doughs.

In the process of the fermentation we obtain a thick product with a pronounced cultured milk aroma that enhances the flavor of dishes with the addition of butter, such as pancakes, pies or mashed potatoes.

json.title: European-style butter
json.text: European butter can boast about its high fat content of 82% to 90%. The high fat content with longer-lasting whipping and live cultures gives European butter a bright yellow color and rich flavor that is instantly transferred to bakery products.

Any butter is made from cream. But depending on the origin of the cream, the composition of the butter and ways of preparation, there are several varieties that ensure different tastes of meals and serve for different purposes:

json.title: Sweet Cream Butter (Unsalted Butter)
json.text: It is the most popular variety due to its versatility: it can be used both for frying vegetables, meat, and for making desserts and pastries. It is made only from cream of animal origin.

json.title: Salted Butter
json.text: Unsalted butter is all cream, while the salted variety has some salt added. Salt acts as a preservative, so this variety of butter lasts longer than the unsalted one. Most often, it is used for spreading on bread, topping veggies and pasta.

runny texture — 0.8 g / 500 ml

thick texture — 5 g / 500 ml

json.title: Agar
json.text:
The shelf life of agar varies from 2 to 3 years since the date of packaging. It is indicated on the packaging and may change depending on the formula and production technology of agar by a specific manufacturer.

Agar should be stored in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight, in airtight packaging.

- Products with agar

1. Agar-based confectionery products are stored about 24 to 36 hours at a temperature between +4 to -8°C
2. Fruit mixtures — up to 7 days in the refrigerator
3. Jam and other preservation — up to 1 month in a cool, dry place, protected from sunlight

json.title: Gelatin
json.text:
Gelatin has a lower density after cooling than agar, so it is suitable for making more delicate desserts. If you want to get a dense and smooth texture, it is better to use agar.

In general, these thickeners can be considered interchangeable, but it should be kept in mind that the gelling ability of agar is much higher than that of gelatin.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. gelatin

ℹ It’s not suitable for vegetarians, as gelatin is made from the bones and tendons of animals

json.title: Pectin
json.text:
Pectin is the most beneficial and equivalent substitute for agar, but there are exceptions. Both products have the vegetal nature and the only difference is that pectin contains carbohydrates, and its calorie content is higher than that of agar.

A prerequisite for the "activation" of pectin is the presence of sugar. Accordingly, substitute agar for pectin in the making of sugar-free desserts is impossible.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2-3 tsp. pectin

json.title: Corn Starch

Agar-agar can be substituted for starch. However, starch makes the filling opaque, when dissolved, that significantly narrows the range of its possibilities.

- Substitute: 1 tsp. agar = 2 tsp. starch

json.text:

json.title: Gelatin — 2

Sometimes when we want our filling to get the properties of 2 different thickeners at once, we add gelatin or agar-agar to the pectin.

For example, when making the Kiwi-Lime-Bergamot cheesecake, the photo of which you can see in the carousel, I used both pectin (to give light elasticity and natural taste) and agar-agar (for stability) to prepare the Mojito marmalade made from vermouth, lime juice and bergamot.

In this case, the gelatin can’t be used to stabilize (gel) the mixture. Can you guess why?

json.title: By chemical properties
json.text:
During the production, pectin undergoes an esterification process — it interacts with alcohol and acid, which gives it various properties.

- Low ester (the degree of esterification (DE) is less than 50%) — is able to gel regardless of the acidity of fruits/berries or amount of sugar, but in the presence of calcium ions.

This type of pectin works with dairy-based and low sugar mixtures.

- High ester (DE is 50% or more) — is able to gel at high acidity (low pH) and high sugar content of the mixture. This is the most popular type of pectin — it dissolves faster in water and gels mixtures faster.

In the pastry business, high ester pectin is used to make zephyr, fruit pastes (pastila) and marmalade.

- Amidated pectin is a low ester pectin which undergoes ammonia treatment during the manufacturing process. Gelation requires less calcium in neutral pH mixtures and is less prone to setting (gelling) at high calcium concentrations.

Amidated pectin is often used to make fruit fillings for yogurts and thermostable fillings.

json.title: Thermal reversibility
json.text:
- Thermoreversible - such pectin becomes liquid when heated and then solidifies when cooled, that is, the mixture can be reheated and cooled again until set.

- Regular - once it gels, it cannot be reheated because pectin loses its properties at temperatures above 90-100 °C.

- Time of setting (gelling)

json.title: Rapid set pectin
json.text:
- degree of esterification - above 70-76%
- gelling temperature - 75-85°С
- gelling time — 10-15 minutes

json.title: Medium rapid set pectin
json.text:
- degree of esterification - 70-72%
- gelling temperature - 60-70°С
- gelling time — 15-20 minutes

json.title: Slow set pectin
json.text:
- degree of esterification - 56-68%
- gelling temperature - 45-60°С
- gelling time - 20-25 minutes

If we try to analyze these numbers, we can notice a consistent pattern:

- The higher the degree of esterification is, the faster the gelling happens, and the higher the temperature is needed to form gel.

The speed of gelation is regulated by chemical compounds in the composition of pectin.

Each manufacturer "plays" with pectin compositions and forms its own assortment. On the one hand, this allows you to choose pectin for absolutely any confectionery purposes, on the other hand, it complicates the issue of their interchangeability.

- Apple or citrus pectin

This is basic, regular pectin. It is obtained from the peels, seeds and pulp of citrus fruits. Has nothing but pectin in its composition. This pectin is classified as high ester, that is, to form a stable gel, this type of pectin needs a large amount of sugar in the composition, the presence of acid and high temperature.

In the previous posts we’ve already discussed such main types of pectin as regular pectin (apple / citrus / yellow), pectin NH, NH Plus and pectin Nappage. Today I suggest analyzing the remaining three types:

json.title: Pectin FX
json.text:
Low ester pectin, which only works with calcium-containing foods; the level of acidity does not matter. Most often it is used to make milk and cream fillings, marmalade or confiture.

- It also works with dairy products regardless of the amount of sugar in the mixture, which allows you to get a non-sweet, balanced taste of creamy fillings.

json.title: Acid-free pectin
json.text:
In fact, this is an analogue of regular pectin, for which the level of acidity does not matter since it contains calcium sulfate which has good hygroscopic, stabilizing and emulsifying properties.

It is used when working with fruits and berries that do not contain acid, e.g. bananas, apples, coconuts, dates, watermelon, etc. It also works well with nut butters. For instance, the pistachio paste marmalade is made using acid-free pectin.

json.title: Slow set pectin — 2
json.text:
Another analogue of regular pectin. The key difference between them is that slow set pectin gels mixtures much more slowly. This is very convenient if, for example, you need to pour a filling or marmalade into small molds - it gives you 3-4 minutes for this, while any other pectin sets almost instantly.

Knowing the properties of each type of pectin, you can easily choose the right one for any of your confectionery experiments and thus, obtain the best result.

Today we’ll talk about ways of adding pectin to the mixture being gelled and will choose the best of them.

1.Pre-dissolve pectin in boiling water

Add pectin powder to boiling water, carefully processing it with a hand blender. Then pour it in a thin stream into the hot mixture being gelled, stirring it with a whisk.

This method is used if the mixture can "hold" additional liquid. It's more suitable for large productions.

Pectin - 5-8%
Water - 92-95%

2. Pre-dissolve pectin in sugar syrup

Add pectin to the sugar syrup and stir thoroughly until the pectin has completely dissolved. Then add it to the mixture being gelled.

3. Mix pectin and sugar

This is the most common and convenient way. Vigorously stirring the warm mixture (35-50 °C) with a whisk, gradually sprinkle in the sugar, pre-mixed with pectin.

- Bear in mind that at temperatures below 35 °C, pectin may start to set, form lumps, and thus, it will be difficult to stir the mixture and get a good texture.

- Why is it necessary to mix sugar and pectin, and not add them separately?

The whole trick is the interaction of pectin with water.

A particle of pectin powder, once in water, absorbs it like a sponge, increasing in size several times, and only after reaching a certain size starts to dissolve.

If pectin powder particles, when in contact with water, are close to each other, then, in the process of absorbing water and swelling, they stick together, forming a sticky lump that slowly dissolves in water. To avoid this, pectin should be pre-mixed with sugar in a ratio of 1:10 or more.

You can know everything about pectins, but when it comes to creating some kind of filling or dessert using it, the question arises: how to decide how much pectin to use?

Among the huge number of questions about pectin, this is perhaps one of the most important.

Let's find the answer

To start the gelling process, you need 3 components:

1. sugar
2. pectin
3. acid or calcium

Scientists consider the ratio 60 : 1 : 1 to be optimal

- 60 parts of sugar
- 1 part of pectin
- 1 part of acid (citric, tartaric, lactic, etc.)

However, this ratio may vary depending on:

- the type of pectin you are using (yellow, NH, FX);
- pectin formula, which each manufacturer keeps in strict confidence;
- the initial content of pectin in berries or fruits that you are going to use;

- the more pectin the fruit you work with contains, the less pectin you need to introduce additionally

- photo 3 shows a table with pectin content in fruits, berries and vegetables

- the type and density of the filling you want to get: runny sauce (coulis), stable and soft cake filling, dense marmalade, thick confiture...
- the type of sugar you are using (sucrose, glucose or fructose).

- You can obtain the most dense texture by using sucrose (regular sugar), and the least dense - by using fructose.

- 4th photo shows the thickness of gel depending on the type of sugar used

Taking into account all the above factors, which the amount of added pectin depends on, it becomes clear that, unfortunately, it is impossible to create a single table with universal proportions of pectin.

But there is good news - most often it is enough just to read the recommendations on the ratio on the packaging, if you have one available.

If not, use the ratio 60 : 1 : 1, take into account all the influencing factors and experiment

Today we will talk about the disinfection of eggs. This topic is important and interesting for all pastry professionals: both home bakers and those who work in production.

First of all, it is worth noting that the disinfection of eggs at home and in production is very different.

- Egg disinfection in production

In production, eggs are disinfected in special rooms. First, the eggs are sorted, randomly ovoscoped (using a special device with a beam of light passing through the egg so that one is able to see what happens inside), and then transferred to 4-section baths for disinfection. In each section, the egg goes through a certain stage:

- 1st section - the eggs are placed in warm water for 5-10 minutes
- 2d section - disinfection with a 0.5% sodium carbonate solution (at 40-45 °C) for 5-10 minutes
- 3d section - disinfection with a 2% bleach solution or 0.5% chloramine solution for 5 minutes
- 4th section - the eggs are rinsed with running water for 5 minutes.

json.title: Egg disinfection at home
json.text:
There are a large number of disinfectants that are suitable for disinfecting eggs at home. For example, Nettex, Battles, Defra and others.

Regular washing with baking soda will not fully protect against the risk of salmonella infection. Moreover, such a procedure will destroy the protective shell of the egg, and the risk of pathogens entering will increase significantly.

In addition, when cooking curds, custards and egg white creams made from raw eggs, the temperature is not high enough to sterilize the eggs. Therefore, there is always a small, but still possible risk of getting infected with salmonella.

However, if you are very meticulous in this matter, there are 3 ways:

1. Do not cook homemade custards and curds made from raw eggs.
2. Always use disinfectants.
3. Switch to pasteurized eggs or dried powder (dried egg white or egg powder).

- may be subject to microbiological deterioration (formation of mold, fungus)
- to obtain a rich color, a large amount of coloring is required
- the color is quite difficult to predict (if the same plants grow on different soils, different shades can be obtained)

json.title: Synthetic
json.text:
Synthetic colorings are chemical compounds that are synthesized in laboratories and used to color various confectionery products, such as frostings, syrups, culinary mastic, sponge cakes, macarons and chocolate.

Pros:
- stable and predictable result
- long shelf life
- a wide range of colors, that allows you to create very bright, saturated shades with a small amount of coloring
- resistance to technological processing (the color won’t fade in the oven and retain its initial shade in frostings of various properties)
- neutral taste

Cons:
- deprived of useful properties
- contain substances of chemical origin in the composition
- stain the oral cavity

Personally, I use both synthetic and natural coloring, depending on the situation, but I try to give preference to natural ones.

json.title: Water-soluble
Fat-soluble
json.text:
Fat-soluble colorings do an excellent job of coloring high-fat mixtures without forming lumps and curdling, giving the desired color to products.

Are a good choice for coloring chocolate used for decoration, creating velour mixtures, chocolates design, etc. Everything containing cocoa butter and chocolate requires the use of fat-soluble colorings.

- Liquid / gel fat-soluble colorings are represented by a very poor color range. Therefore, compatible colorings were created (when mixed with a water-soluble coloring, they turn it into a fat-soluble one).

- dry (powder) fat-soluble colorings are added to chocolate in dry form and should be thoroughly mixed or processed with an emulsion blender.

- Which coloring is better for chocolate: liquid or powder?

Definitely powder! The liquid will inevitably break the structure of cocoa butter, and you might encounter issues when tempering the mixture.

The powder coloring will not affect the mixture in any way, but the weight of the coloring cannot exceed 0.02% of the weight of the product being colored in order to avoid staining the oral cavity.

json.title: PART 2 — 2
json.text:
#marusya_flavours

Judging by the number of "5" under the previous post, the topic turned out to be interesting for you. Knowing tastes and having the ability to understand and combine them skillfully is incredibly important both in creating desserts and meals in your kitchen!

As promised, today I will dwell upon the 4 main tastes.

json.title: Sweet taste
json.text:
To act on our receptors, a large amount of a sweet substance is needed, unlike other tastes. Nevertheless, we can appreciate the harmony and pleasant taste that even a subtle sweet taste gives to spicy dishes.

Sweet taste is combined with bitter (chocolate), sour (berries, lemon) and even salty (caramel). Sweetness can also bring out the flavors of other ingredients, like fruit or mint.

json.title: Salty taste
json.text: Salt is a natural flavor enhancer and the most important ingredient for making spicy food delicious. By the way, sugar plays this role in desserts.

json.title: Sour taste
json.text: As flavor enhancers, acidic components are second in importance only to salt in spicy dishes and sugar in sweet ones. Sour notes - whether it be a little lemon juice or vinegar - add brightness to the dish. The harmonious combination of sourness with other flavors is crucial to the finished dish.

json.title: Bitter taste
json.text:
Humans are most sensitive to bitter taste, and our body's defense mechanisms allow it to be recognized even in small amounts.

The bitter taste is harmoniously combined with the sweet, and sometimes can significantly reduce the richness of the dish. For some chefs, the bitter taste is more important than others, but some see it as a necessary savory flavor - one that makes you take another bite, and then another.

Every delicious dish you've ever tasted has been the result of these 4 tastes acting on your taste buds. We distinguish them both individually and in combination.
part 3

the beginning can be found by the hashtag #marusya_flavours

We continue to talk about tastes. Today I will tell you about the fifth little-known taste of umami, and also we will deal with such a concept as "taste perception".

json.title: Umami (found in high-protein foods)
json.text:
In addition to the four basic tastes, a growing body of evidence points to the existence of a fifth taste, umami.

It gives dishes a salty or meaty "rich" taste. It can be felt in ingredients such as anchovies, cheese, mushrooms, green tea, and flavorings such as monosodium glutamate, which is the main component of ready-made seasonings.

json.title: Temperature — 2
json.text:
Temperature is the main sensation perceived by the oral cavity. The temperature of food even affects how we perceive its taste. For example, cool temperatures suppress the appeal of sweetness.

The temperature of food can affect both how it is perceived and how much you enjoy it. The menu is always dominated by hot dishes in winter and chilled ones on hot summer days, precisely because they balance the temperature of our body and the environment.

json.title: Texture
json.text:
The texture of food plays a crucial role in its ability to attract and please. We consider mashed and/or creamy foods (soup, mashed potatoes) traditional while crunchy food is considered fun.

We like texture because it activates the senses of touch, sight, and sound.

part 4

the beginning can be found by the hashtag #marusya_flavours

Thank you for supporting new posts about tastes with likes and comments! I see that you’re involved and interested and it inspires me to write a continuation.

So, in addition to temperature and texture, the following 2 factors also affect the TASTE PERCEPTION:

json.title: Piquancy
json.text: Our taste buds can also perceive what we mistakenly call spicy, meaning piquant taste, that is more pronounced in chili peppers and barely noticeable in cayenne pepper powder. Some prefer the piquant taste to others.

json.title: Astringent taste
json.text: Our taste buds also recognize astringency, a dry mouth sensation caused by the tannin content in tea or wine, and sometimes cranberries, unripe persimmons, and certain types of nuts.

json.title: Strong spicy taste
json.text: Ingredients such as horseradish and mustard have a strong spicy taste and aroma. However, despite their piquancy, their taste and aroma irritate the receptors of both the nasal and oral cavities.

json.title: Chemical senses
json.text: The term “chemical senses” refers to taste sensations that are pleasant to us (for example, the tingling sensation when drinking sparkling drinks) and at the same time irritate or deceive the taste buds (for example, chili pepper creates a false sensation of burning, while peppermint has a cooling effect).

tips.title: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT GELATIN — 2

json.title: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT GELATIN — 2
json.text:
At first glance, the topic is very simple and there is not much to learn about, but, in fact, it’s not that easy.

Gelatin (French gélatine, from Latin gelātus "frozen") is a mixture of peptides and proteins produced by partial hydrolysis of collagen extracted from the skin, bones and connective tissues of animals. The collagen (protein) in these tissues is converted to gluten.

Gelatin is used in many areas. If we talk about cooking, then it is used to make jelly, confit, mousse, soufflé, marshmallows and so on.

Thanks to it, the mousse cakes keep their shape and tender creams in eclairs are not runny. Gelatin is also used for the production of ice cream to prevent sugar crystallization and reduce protein coagulation.

Edible gelatin used to be a product of animal origin, but with the development of the technologies there have appeared different variations of gelatin that no one could think about.

Notice, now gelatin can be made using a by-products of:

- beef
- pork
- fish
- vegetables

You will also find halal and kosher gelatin.

- Types of gelatin

There are two types of gelatin – powdered and sheet.

json.title: POWDERED — 2
json.text:
It is always soaked in cold water in a ratio of 1: 5 or, depending on the strength of the gelatin, 1: 6.

Mostly, it’s "instant gelatin" – it takes just a few minutes for it to swell. Then it is heated until it is completely dissolved.

It is important that the liquid to which the gelatin is added is warm, so that the gelatin disperses well in it, and does not form a huge lump.

Sometimes it is difficult and irrational to heat up the entire mousse or cream. For example, if it's a mousse made with cold sour cream, then a part of it, no more than 1/3, is taken, slightly heated over a water bath or in a microwave, then the gelatin is added to it, mixed well, and then both mixtures – the warm with gelatin and the cold one – are combined.

json.title: CAKE COATING. COMMON PROBLEMS — 2
json.text:
How to avoid air bubbles?

I’m sure you sometimes come across photos of assembled cakes with packs of butter or cream on top.

I hope you’ve already guessed why this is necessary, but in a few words I’ll explain what happens.

Being pressed down by some weight, all the air comes out of the cake, and in this way you let the layers tightly stick together for a more secure transportation of the product.

So let's see whether it is obligatory to put a weight on a cake, or such an idea is completely meaningless?

Let's start with where we started.

What to do if air bubbles appear on the side of the cake over time? Answer: put on a press!

There are some simple rules for placing a cake under the press:

- the press does not have to be put on for long - several hours will be quite enough, depending on the thickness of your cake and the weight of the press itself

- the press is never put directly on the cake, but always on a thick cake base to evenly distribute pressure over the entire surface

- the press should be put only on the cake which is tightly tightened with the acetate film, or, better with a cake ring for assembling.

- It’s better not to use a press for cakes with very delicate and moist fillings.

- Pros of putting a cake under the press:

- no air inside the cake and, as a result, no bubbles on coating
- perfectly flat cake surface, which greatly facilitates the smoothing process
- perfectly even layers in the cut, which guarantees a wow effect when cutting

- Cons of putting a cake under the press:

- if you put a too heavy press / leave the press for a long time / put the press on a very delicate filling, then you can end up with a too tamped cake.

\Yesterday we discussed the possible reasons why the filling may get out of the cake in the form of bubbles on the coating:

- not verified, inaccurate recipe
- you deviated from the cooking instructions
- incorrect assembly of the cake.

But what if you are 200% confident in your filling and, nevertheless, a tricky bubble still has appeared on your finished cake? Or, let’s say, you have pierced the bubble and found that ... there is nothing there!

But it cannot be empty, can it? There should have been something inside that pushed the buttercream and formed the bubble! And if this is not a filling, then, of course, it is ... air!

Let's figure out where this air comes from, what it does inside the cake and why it starts to get out at the most inopportune moment.

Air gets inside the cake, naturally, during the assembly process. When we assemble a cake, especially without a cake ring, we very carefully lower each sponge layer on top of the filling with frosting, trying not to press too much, otherwise we risk squeezing the filling with the frosting out.

It is quite natural that many hollows, filled with air, remain inside the cake. What happens next? In the process of maturing, thanks to the gravity, our cake "shrinks", pushing all the air out.

But it often happens that not all the air has time to get out and some of it remains inside the cake, looking for a perfect moment to put a pastry chef on edge. Usually, because it tries to get out when the chef is about to give the cake to the client.

A similar problem often happens with sponge cakes, especially if we don’t give the assembled cake enough time to rest before applying the coating.

tips.title: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT GELATIN — 3

json.title: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT GELATIN — 3
json.text:
Judging by the number of questions that I often receive, articles with an analysis of the ingredients are very relevant for many of you.

So here is the continuation about gelatin and I kindly ask you to support it with any comment.

A bloomed mixture of water and powdered gelatin is called a gelatin mass.

This term is often found in the recipes of famous chefs. It's very convenient: you make gelatin mass in advance and put it in the fridge, and when you need it, you take it out, weigh the required amount and use it.

The gelatin mass can be stored for up to a week. We’ll talk about it in more detail a little later.

tips.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 2

json.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 2
json.text:
Personally, I prefer the hot infusion, since it is much more effective and does not require such a long preparation.

The hot method suggests heating the whipping cream / milk with flavoring up to 90 °C / 194 °F over low heat. Then you should cover the mixture with a lid and let it infuse for at least 2-3 hours. For an intense flavor, you may repeat the process one more time.

If you use flowers, leaves, coffee grains, tonka beans or tea as a flavoring, it’s a good idea to process the whipping cream together with the flavoring with a blender before heating.

But in this case you should increase the amount of whipping cream / milk by 30-40%, and after infusion simply strain the mass through a strainer or a piece of cheesecloth.

ℹOnly a metal cake pan with a removable bottom is good for baking cheesecake.

At first glance, this is a correct statement, because in this case unmolding the cheesecake can be done with your eyes shut. In fact, cheesecakes can be baked equally well in cake pans with removable bottom and in baking rings.

Just when dealing with baking rings, beginners will immediately face two seemingly difficult tasks:

- how to shape and then transfer a cheesecake in a baking ring without a bottom, because after baking the dessert is unstable and requires careful treatment.

There are several solutions to this problem.

In order to easily transfer the cheesecake to the oven and then to the fridge, you can place the baking ring on the bottom of the old split cake mold of a slightly larger diameter, covered with a sheet of parchment paper.

I use another method - I wrap the bottom of the baking ring in several layers of foil and put it on a thick cake base.

You can, of course, put the ring directly on the baking sheet, provided that its surface is perfectly flat, but in this case you will not be able to use it until the cheesecake is completely cooled. To be continued.

- how to unmold a seemingly glued cheesecake from a baking ring without destroying its ideal shape.

Firstly, remember to apply a thin layer of oil (I prefer coconut oil) on the baking ring and unmold the cheesecake out only after 6 hours of cooling.

Secondly, if you leave a cheesecake at room temperature for 15-20 minutes, the oil will slightly melt and you will only need to carefully lift the baking ring up. The cheesecake will remain on the cake base.

- Useful tips:

- To speed up the process of unmolding the cheese, you may heat the baking ring up with a heat gun or a hair dryer.

- Preferably, the cheesecake should not be higher than 6 cm (without décor).

- Try to shape the sides of the shortbread shell so that the cheese mass is only slightly below the level of the sides, otherwise it may detach slightly after baking.

ℹCheesecake must be baked at low temperatures (not higher than 120 °C / 248 °F) with a water bath.

Let me remind you that a water bath is a baking sheet full of boiling water installed on the lowest level of the oven.

Please, pay your attention to the fact that you should not pour water into the baking sheet with the cheesecake, otherwise the water will get into the mold and your cheesecake will get wet.
In fact, the baking mode for a cheesecake depends on the characteristics of your oven. Cheesecakes can be baked at either 90-100 °C / 194-212 °F or 150-160 °C / 302-320 °F, with or without a water bath.

If you bake your cheesecake at a very low temperature (90-100 °C / 194-212 °F), then you probably won't need a water bath. But if your oven is so powerful that even at 90 °C / 194 °F the cheesecake rises and its top burns - put a water bath - it lowers the heat in the oven.

I used to bake cheesecakes with a water bath and strictly at a temperature not more than 120 °C / 248 °F. It would take my cheesecakes at least 3-4 hours to bake, and for a long time I could not understand what I was doing wrong.

Then a brilliant idea came across my mind and I bought a thermometer for the oven. It turned out that my 120 °C / 248 °F + a water bath = 80-90 °C / 176-194 °F of real temperature. Now, when baking a cheesecake with a water bath, I set the temperature to at least 150 °C / 302 °F and my thermometer shows exactly 120 °C / 248 °F. The cheesecake is ready in 1.5 hours!

ℹYou can bake cheesecakes using absolutely any oven mode.

It all depends on the situation, and, again, on the characteristics of your oven. If the top heating element heats too much, then turn on only the bottom one. In 80% of cases, conventional heating is the best option. If you need to bake several trays at the same time, use the convection mode.

If you have difficulties with the baking mode and the uniformity of baking, you can cover the top of the cheesecake with foil. This will keep the light color of the cheesecake and prevent it from being burnt.

- Add the flavouring directly to the cheese mass.

- What could it be?

- berry, fruit purees
- whole berries and fruit pieces
- caramel, dulce de leche
- chocolate, ganache, Nutella
- nuts and nut paste
- instant coffee, matcha tea
- liqueurs, cognac and other alcoholic beverages.

You need to work very carefully, since each of these flavourings has a different water and sugar content. The most important advice I want to give is that berry or fruit purees should be pre-thickened with cornstarch.

Add the starch to the puree and constantly stirring bring it to a boil - you should get a thick mass. It is also possible to go without pre-cooking, but then the texture of the cheesecake will be a little softer.

If you add alcohol, then reduce the cream / milk in the recipe by the same amount, if you do not want the cheesecake to be very tender.

- Infuse cream or milk.

- You may infuse it with:

- cinnamon stick, vanilla pod, saffron, whole star anise, cardamom, or any other spice
- lavender and violets flowers, rose petals
- leaves of mint, lemon balm, basil, thyme
- coffee beans
- tonka beans
- lemon, orange or lime zest
- green, black, milk or any other tea
- blue cheeses and more.

There are two ways of infusion- cold and hot one.

As for the cold method, it is enough to add flavoring to the cream / milk and leave it overnight, or even better for a day, in the fridge.

tips.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 3

json.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 3
json.text:
I am glad that you find the tips on making the perfect cheesecake useful, so I will be happy to continue. If you like this idea, leave + in the comments!

ℹIs it necessary to use room temperature ingredients to make the cheese filling?

No, it won’t affect the taste, the texture or the look of the pastry in any way. In fact, only the temperature of the cream cheese matters, because when the cream cheese is at room temperature, it is much softer and then it’s easier to mix the mass until smooth, avoiding lumps.

Useful tip:

- If you forgot to get the cream cheese out of the fridge beforehand, you may slightly heat it up over a water bath or in the microwave oven.

ℹDo not whip the mass for a long time, otherwise there might be cracks on the surface of the cheesecake due to the excess of air in the mass. Work at low speed.

In fact, it is enough to understand that the cheesecake should be mixed until smooth, and not whipped until fluffy.

As for the cracks that appear due to air bubbles, I'm sure this is more of a myth. There were several cases when I used cold cream cheese and overwhipped the cheese mass trying to get rid of the lumps. There were bubbles, but no cracks.

The reason for the formation of cracks on the surface of the cheesecake is actually very simple - the baking temperature is too high, but I will write about it in detail later in the article.

- Useful tip:

It is better to introduce the eggs into the cheese filling one at a time, each time mixing the mass until smooth.

tips.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 4

json.title: HOW TO MAKE A PERFECT CHEESECAKE — 4
json.text:
I suggest paying closer attention to this popular American dessert and trying to figure out together which rules for its preparation should be considered as indisputable facts, and which can be neglected.

Also, in this article, I will share some tips that will help you to make not only incredibly delicious, but also gorgeous-looking cheesecake.

Let’s bust the myths! And I’ll start with making the shortbread crust.

ℹThe crust can be made using the ready-made or home-made shortbread cookies, you won't notice much difference.

Although I completely agree with the first part of the statement, the second seems quite controversial. If you want to make a really delicious cheesecake, do not be too lazy to bake home-made sables with almond or hazelnut flour.

Useful tips:

- While forming the base of the cheesecake, try to distribute the crust along the bottom and sides of the springform pan in an even layer. Mind the thickness of the sides and the bottom, it should be the same.

- Make sure that the edges are not thick. To avoid this common problem, do the sides first, and only then proceed to the bottom.

- It is very convenient to use a flat bottom mug (not the one with the concave bottom) with sides at right angle for forming the cheesecake base. Also, a tablespoon might be quite helpful.

- If after baking the sides of the shortbread crust have slid down, replace the butter with a thicker one and try to use less of it.

- It is much easier and faster not to bake the formed shortbread crust, but simply put it in the freezer for 30-60 minutes.

- If you use the coconut oil instead of butter for the reconstituted shortbread crust, the base will come out crispier and crumblier, and it will be easier to unmold it.

json.title: Flavor Description
json.text:
sweet "candy"
 nice acidity
 top fruity notes
 light creamy aftertaste
 caramel notes
 inherent oiliness

Strawberries can be leading — then you need weaker flavors that emphasize the intensity of its taste, sweetness. If strawberries are as addition, beat the leading flavor with spices or heat treatment.

json.title: Aroma Profile
json.text:
fruity aroma
 sweet caramel notes
 light grassiness
 spicy notes of vanilla
 strong resemblance to tomato aromatics

The aroma profile of strawberries is composed of over 360 components, including esters, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, terpenes, furanones, and sulfur compounds. The aroma of ripe strawberries is recognized as one of the most complex fruit flavors.

Pairs well with:

- nuts — almonds, cashews, pistachios and pecans. The ideal nutty companion — hazelnuts — does not overlap the taste of strawberries, but gently complements it.

- other fruits and berries such as orange, pineapple, melon, raspberry, coconut

The flavor combination strawberry-tomato deserves special attention — the natural flavor of strawberries is very similar to the aromatics of tomatoes, so the presence of tomatoes in dessert tarts, stracciatella and bruschettas is increasingly being traced

- spices, herbs and seasonings — vanilla, cinnamon, mint, ginger, lemongrass and... balsamic vinegar! Just a couple of drops of balsamic can greatly enhance the taste of strawberries. The combination is often used by chefs in salads, tarts.

- dairy products – cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, cream, mascarpone, cream cheese
- Strawberry-Soft Cheeses — strawberries have soft, creamy, buttery notes in their flavor, making them a great partner for soft milk, creamy, cheeses and cottage cheese.
